name: CBT
what: A structured, time-limited talking therapy that looks at how thoughts, feelings, physical sensations and behaviour affect one another. You learn to notice unhelpful patterns of thinking and acting, test them against evidence, and try out new ways of responding, so that problems become more manageable in the present.
origin: Developed by Aaron T. Beck at the University of Pennsylvania in the 1960s, building on behaviour therapy and Albert Ellis's earlier rational approach; later expanded into many problem-specific versions in the US and UK.
evidence: One of the most researched psychological therapies, supported by many randomised trials and meta-analyses for depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD, insomnia and other problems. Effects are typically moderate and comparable to other well-delivered therapies; not everyone benefits and relapse occurs.
practice: Usually individual, sometimes group or guided self-help; typically 6 to 20 weekly sessions of about 50 to 60 minutes. You and the therapist agree goals, set an agenda each session, and do homework such as thought records or behavioural experiments. Delivered by psychologists, CBT therapists and other trained clinicians.
suitability: Widely used for depression, anxiety disorders, panic, OCD, PTSD, insomnia and some long-term health conditions. NICE recommends CBT for depression (NG222) and generalised anxiety disorder (CG113), among others. It may suit people less well if they do not want a structured, homework-based approach.
cautions: Quality varies with training; check accreditation. Being asked to face difficult thoughts or situations can be temporarily distressing.
uk: Free via NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral in England) and NHS mental health services; privately through practitioners accredited by BABCP or on PSA-accredited registers.

name: DBT
what: A form of cognitive behavioural therapy designed for people who experience very intense emotions and self-harm or suicidal urges. It balances acceptance of the person as they are with active change, and teaches skills in mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and getting on with other people.
origin: Developed by Marsha Linehan at the University of Washington, Seattle, during the late 1980s; treatment manuals published in 1993.
evidence: Several randomised trials show DBT reduces self-harm and suicidal behaviour and improves functioning in people with borderline personality disorder, though effects vary and trials are often small. An adolescent version (DBT-A) has some trial support for reducing self-harm. Evidence for other conditions is more limited.
practice: A comprehensive programme usually runs about a year: weekly individual therapy, a weekly skills group of around two hours, telephone coaching between sessions, and a therapist consultation team. Shorter skills-only groups also exist. Delivered by teams of trained clinicians.
suitability: Mainly used for borderline personality disorder and recurrent self-harm. NICE says a comprehensive DBT programme may be considered for women with BPD for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority (CG78), and DBT-A for young people with frequent self-harm and emotional dysregulation (NG225). It is demanding and needs commitment.
cautions: Full programmes are intensive and waiting lists can be long; skills-only or partial versions may not match trial results.
uk: Mainly through NHS community mental health and specialist personality disorder services; some private and independent providers; practitioners may hold BABCP or other accredited-register membership.

name: ACT
what: A behavioural therapy that, rather than trying to change or get rid of painful thoughts and feelings, helps people make room for them and step back from them. The aim is psychological flexibility: being present and acting in line with what you value, even when difficult experiences are there.
origin: Developed by Steven C. Hayes with Kelly Wilson and Kirk Strosahl in the United States, from work in the 1980s; the main treatment book appeared in 1999. Linked to relational frame theory.
evidence: Many randomised trials and meta-analyses show benefits for chronic pain, depression, anxiety and some health conditions, generally similar to established CBT rather than better. Study quality is mixed, with many small trials.
practice: Individual or group, often 8 to 16 sessions of about an hour, also in workshops, books and apps. Sessions use metaphors, mindfulness exercises and values clarification, with practice between sessions. Delivered by psychologists and other trained therapists.
suitability: Used for chronic pain, depression, anxiety, stress and coping with long-term illness. NICE says ACT or CBT for pain may be considered for people aged 16 and over with chronic primary pain (NG193). It may suit less well those wanting a direct focus on challenging specific thoughts.
uk: Offered in some NHS pain, psychology and Talking Therapies services; widely available privately from clinical psychologists and therapists on HCPC or PSA-accredited registers.

name: REBT
aka: Rational emotive behavior therapy; earlier called rational therapy and rational emotive therapy (RET)
what: An early form of cognitive behavioural therapy built on the idea that it is not events themselves but rigid beliefs about them, such as 'I must' or 'I can't stand it', that cause much emotional distress. Therapist and client actively dispute these beliefs and replace them with more flexible, accepting ones.
origin: Founded by psychologist Albert Ellis in New York in the mid-1950s; first called rational therapy, renamed rational emotive therapy in 1961 and rational emotive behaviour therapy in 1993.
evidence: Meta-analyses suggest REBT reduces distress across a range of problems, but many studies are small, older or of limited quality. It has far less recent trial evidence than standard CBT and is not separately named in NICE guidance.
practice: Usually individual, sometimes group or workshop; often 5 to 20 weekly sessions. The therapist takes a direct, teaching style, using the ABC model (activating event, beliefs, consequences), vigorous questioning of beliefs and homework. Delivered by CBT therapists and counsellors.
suitability: Used for anxiety, depression, anger, guilt, low self-worth and performance or workplace stress, and in coaching. Its confrontational style may not suit people who prefer a gentler or more exploratory approach.
uk: Mainly via private practitioners and some CBT services; therapists may be BABCP-accredited or on PSA-accredited registers. Not usually offered by name in the NHS.

name: Behavioral Activation
what: A structured therapy for depression that focuses on what people do rather than what they think. Depression tends to shrink activity, which deepens low mood; BA helps you track activities and mood, notice avoidance, and gradually schedule meaningful and enjoyable activities to rebuild contact with rewarding parts of life.
origin: Rooted in Peter Lewinsohn's behavioural work on depression in the US in the 1970s; developed as a stand-alone therapy after Neil Jacobson's 1996 study, with a manual by Christopher Martell and colleagues in 2001.
evidence: Many randomised trials and meta-analyses show behavioural activation works for depression about as well as CBT. A large UK trial found it could be delivered effectively and more cheaply by junior mental health workers.
practice: Individual or group, usually 8 to 20 sessions. You keep activity and mood diaries, identify patterns of avoidance, set small graded goals and solve problems that get in the way. Delivered by psychologists, CBT therapists and trained practitioners, including psychological wellbeing practitioners.
suitability: Mainly used for depression, including in older adults and people with long-term conditions. NICE recommends individual and group behavioural activation as options for depression (NG222). It may suit people who prefer practical work to discussing thoughts.
uk: Available free through NHS Talking Therapies and NHS psychology services; also from private CBT therapists, for example those accredited by BABCP.

name: Exposure Therapy
aka: Includes exposure and response prevention (ERP), systematic desensitisation, graded exposure, in vivo and imaginal exposure
what: A behavioural approach in which people gradually and safely face the situations, objects, memories or sensations they fear and avoid. Staying with the fear, without escaping or using safety behaviours, lets anxiety reduce and teaches that the feared outcome is less likely or more bearable than expected.
origin: Developed from learning theory in the 1950s and 1960s; Joseph Wolpe's systematic desensitisation in South Africa (published 1958) was a major early form, followed by flooding and Victor Meyer's exposure and response prevention for OCD in the UK.
evidence: Strong evidence from many trials and meta-analyses for specific phobias, OCD (as exposure and response prevention), panic, social anxiety and PTSD. It is a core part of most effective CBT treatments for anxiety. Dropout can be higher because it is demanding.
practice: Usually individual, sometimes group or intensive formats; often 8 to 16 sessions, though single long sessions are used for some phobias. You build a ladder of feared situations with the therapist and work up it step by step, in session and as homework. Delivered by CBT therapists and psychologists.
suitability: Used for phobias, OCD, panic, health anxiety, social anxiety and PTSD. NICE recommends CBT including exposure and response prevention for OCD (CG31). It needs willingness to tolerate temporary distress, so pacing is agreed with the client.
cautions: Should be planned with a trained therapist; poorly paced exposure can be distressing. Some physical conditions may need medical advice first.
uk: Delivered within CBT through NHS Talking Therapies and specialist NHS anxiety and OCD services; privately through BABCP-accredited therapists and clinical psychologists.

name: CPT
what: A structured trauma-focused cognitive therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. It helps people examine and change 'stuck points', beliefs about the trauma, such as self-blame, and about safety, trust, power, esteem and intimacy, that keep them from recovering. Some versions include writing a detailed account of the event.
origin: Developed by Patricia Resick and colleagues at the University of Missouri-St Louis in the late 1980s, initially for survivors of rape; manual published in the early 1990s.
evidence: Many randomised trials, including with veterans and sexual assault survivors, show CPT reduces PTSD symptoms, with effects similar to other trauma-focused therapies. Not everyone responds, and dropout is notable in some trials.
practice: Usually 12 weekly individual sessions of about an hour, sometimes in groups or intensive daily formats. You complete worksheets that question unhelpful beliefs and practise between sessions. Delivered by psychologists and trained trauma therapists.
suitability: Used for PTSD after many kinds of trauma. NICE lists CPT among the forms of trauma-focused CBT recommended for adults with PTSD (NG116). It may not suit people who are currently unsafe or in crisis until that is addressed.
cautions: Talking about trauma can temporarily increase distress; it should be delivered by trained clinicians.
uk: Available in some NHS Talking Therapies, NHS trauma and veterans' services (such as Op Courage in England) and from private trauma-trained psychologists.

name: MCT
aka: Not to be confused with metacognitive training for psychosis, also abbreviated MCT
what: A therapy that targets how people think rather than what they think. It holds that prolonged worry, rumination and threat monitoring, driven by beliefs about thinking itself, keep anxiety and depression going. Clients learn to notice thoughts without engaging with them and to reduce worry and rumination.
origin: Developed by Adrian Wells at the University of Manchester, England, from the early 1990s, based on his work with Gerald Matthews on a model of self-regulation and attention.
evidence: A growing number of randomised trials, many from the developer's group, suggest metacognitive therapy is effective for generalised anxiety disorder and depression, sometimes outperforming CBT. Independent replication is more limited and it is not named in NICE guidance.
practice: Usually individual, about 8 to 12 weekly sessions. Work includes attention training exercises, 'detached mindfulness', postponing worry, and challenging beliefs that worry is uncontrollable or helpful. Delivered by psychologists and therapists trained in the method.
suitability: Used mainly for generalised anxiety disorder, depression, PTSD, OCD and health anxiety, especially where worry or rumination is central. It may suit people who have found arguing with thoughts unhelpful.
uk: Available from some NHS psychology services and private practitioners trained through the Metacognitive Therapy Institute; therapists may be BABCP-accredited or HCPC-registered psychologists.
checkNotes: Founding year approximate (early 1990s; S-REF model 1994, GAD model mid-1990s). Strength of independent evidence relative to CBT is debated.

name: Unified Protocol
display: Unified Protocol for Transdiagnostic Treatment of Emotional Disorders (UP)
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is a CBT-based transdiagnostic treatment, so it is placed in cognitive and behavioural.
what: A single cognitive behavioural treatment designed to work across anxiety, depression and related disorders, rather than one manual per diagnosis. It targets shared processes, especially strong negative emotions and attempts to avoid them, through modules on emotional awareness, flexible thinking, reducing avoidance and emotion exposure.
origin: Developed by David H. Barlow and colleagues at Boston University's Center for Anxiety and Related Disorders in the 2000s; first described in 2004, with the treatment manual published in 2011.
evidence: Several randomised trials and meta-analyses show the Unified Protocol works about as well as diagnosis-specific CBT for anxiety disorders and depression. Evidence for other conditions and in routine services is still developing.
practice: Individual or group, typically 12 to 18 weekly sessions of about an hour, with a client workbook. Eight modules include goal-setting, mindful emotion awareness, cognitive flexibility, countering emotional behaviours, facing physical sensations and emotion exposures. Delivered by psychologists and CBT-trained therapists.
suitability: Used for anxiety disorders, depression and people with more than one such problem; adaptations exist for children and adolescents. It may suit services treating mixed presentations. It is not specifically named in NICE guidance.
uk: Used in some NHS and university clinics and research settings; mainly accessible privately from psychologists trained in it.
checkNotes: Family chosen (cb); source states it is not in the trauma family. Availability in UK NHS services is not well documented.

name: Schema Therapy
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it grew out of cognitive therapy, though it integrates attachment, Gestalt and psychodynamic ideas, so it is placed in cognitive and behavioural.
what: An integrative therapy for long-standing emotional and relationship patterns. It proposes that unmet childhood needs create 'schemas', deep beliefs about self and others, and 'modes' that are triggered in adult life. Therapy combines cognitive work, imagery rescripting, chair work and a warm, partly reparenting relationship to meet needs and weaken schemas.
origin: Developed by Jeffrey Young in the United States from the late 1980s, extending Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy; key book published in 1990, with later mode work developed with Dutch colleagues.
evidence: Several randomised trials, mainly in the Netherlands, show benefits for borderline personality disorder, and there is some evidence for other personality disorders and chronic depression. Trials are fewer and smaller than for CBT, and it is not specifically recommended by NICE.
practice: Individual or group, often long-term: weekly sessions for one to three years for personality disorders, fewer for other problems. You map schemas and modes, use imagery and chair dialogues, and practise new behaviours. Delivered by psychologists and therapists certified by the International Society of Schema Therapy.
suitability: Used for personality disorders, especially borderline personality disorder, chronic depression and long-standing relationship difficulties. Its length and emotional intensity may not suit those wanting short-term help.
cautions: Long courses can be costly privately; work on childhood experiences can be distressing.
uk: Offered in some NHS personality disorder and psychology services; mostly privately from therapists certified by the International Society of Schema Therapy, often also HCPC or BABCP registered.

name: FAP
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is a behavioural therapy based on Skinner's behaviour analysis, so it is placed in cognitive and behavioural.
what: A behavioural therapy that uses the relationship between client and therapist as the main place for change. Problems people have in relationships outside therapy are expected to show up in session; the therapist notices them and responds naturally to encourage more open, connected ways of relating.
origin: Developed by Robert Kohlenberg and Mavis Tsai at the University of Washington, Seattle; set out in their 1991 book.
evidence: Mostly case studies, small trials and single-case designs; a few small randomised trials suggest benefits, often when combined with CBT or ACT. Overall the evidence is limited and it is not in NICE guidance.
practice: Individual, sometimes added to another therapy; length varies, typically weekly sessions over months. The therapist pays close attention to what happens between you in the room, invites honest feedback and practising vulnerability and intimacy. Delivered by trained psychologists or therapists.
suitability: Used for interpersonal difficulties, depression, anxiety and personality difficulties, often alongside other approaches. It may not suit people uncomfortable with close focus on the therapy relationship.
uk: Rarely available by name; mainly via private psychologists or therapists with FAP training, often working within ACT or CBT.

name: Problem-Solving
what: A brief, practical talking therapy that teaches a step-by-step method for tackling everyday problems that contribute to stress and low mood. You define a problem, generate possible solutions, weigh them up, choose one, try it and review the result, while also building a more constructive attitude towards problems.
origin: Developed from the work of Thomas D'Zurilla and Marvin Goldfried in the United States, published 1971; later expanded by Arthur and Christine Nezu.
evidence: Meta-analyses show problem-solving therapy reduces depressive symptoms, including in older adults and primary care, with moderate effects. Evidence for anxiety and other problems is smaller and more mixed.
practice: Usually individual, sometimes group or by telephone or online; often 4 to 12 sessions, from 30 minutes to an hour. You work through real current problems with structured worksheets and plan actions between sessions. Delivered by psychologists, nurses, GPs and trained practitioners.
suitability: Used for mild to moderate depression, stress, and people facing practical difficulties, including older adults and those with physical illness. It may suit those wanting a short, practical approach, less so those whose difficulties are mainly long-standing or relational.
uk: Problem-solving is often part of guided self-help and CBT in NHS Talking Therapies; rarely offered as a separate therapy, though some private practitioners use it.

name: App-Based CBT
aka: Digital CBT; internet-delivered CBT (iCBT); computerised CBT (cCBT); digitally enabled therapies
familyNote: The source does not state its family; as CBT delivered through apps and websites it is placed in digital and technology.
what: Cognitive behavioural therapy delivered through a website or smartphone app, often as structured modules with exercises, quizzes and mood tracking. Some programmes are fully self-guided; others include regular support from a practitioner by message or phone. The aim is to make CBT techniques more widely and flexibly available.
origin: Computerised CBT programmes appeared in the UK and elsewhere in the 1990s and early 2000s, for example Beating the Blues; internet and smartphone versions spread from the 2010s.
evidence: Meta-analyses show guided internet-delivered CBT reduces depression and anxiety, with effects close to face-to-face CBT in some trials. Fully self-guided programmes and many commercial apps have weaker evidence and high dropout. Quality varies greatly between products.
practice: Usually individual and self-paced, often 6 to 12 weekly modules of 30 to 60 minutes on a phone or computer, with optional or required practitioner check-ins. You read or watch content, complete exercises and track progress.
suitability: Used for mild to moderate depression, anxiety, insomnia and stress. NICE's early value assessments allow some digitally enabled therapies to be used with practitioner support in NHS Talking Therapies while more evidence is gathered (HTE8, HTE9). It may not suit people in crisis or with severe problems.
cautions: Many apps are unregulated and untested; check data privacy. Not a substitute for urgent help if you are at risk.
uk: Available through NHS Talking Therapies, which uses some NICE-assessed programmes with practitioner support, and as commercial apps of varying quality.
checkNotes: Founding year is approximate (computerised CBT emerged gradually). The specific programmes covered by NICE HTE8/HTE9 change over time.

name: EMDR
what: A structured trauma therapy in which a person briefly recalls a distressing memory while following side-to-side eye movements or other alternating stimulation, such as taps or tones. It is meant to help the memory be processed so that it becomes less vivid and upsetting, alongside more helpful beliefs about oneself.
origin: Developed by American psychologist Francine Shapiro in 1987, first published in 1989, in California.
evidence: Many randomised trials and meta-analyses show EMDR reduces PTSD symptoms, with effects similar to trauma-focused CBT. Whether the eye movements themselves add benefit beyond the exposure and cognitive elements is still debated.
practice: Individual, typically 8 to 12 sessions of 60 to 90 minutes, though this varies. It follows eight phases: history-taking, preparation, assessing a target memory, processing it with bilateral stimulation, and installing positive beliefs. Delivered by clinicians who have completed accredited EMDR training.
suitability: Mainly used for PTSD. NICE recommends EMDR for adults with PTSD who present more than three months after non-combat-related trauma, and it may be considered for children and young people (NG116). Extra preparation may be needed for complex trauma or dissociation.
cautions: Processing memories can be temporarily distressing; it should be delivered by qualified clinicians, and caution is needed with severe dissociation.
uk: Available in NHS Talking Therapies and NHS trauma services, and privately from practitioners accredited by EMDR Association UK, usually also on HCPC or PSA-accredited registers.

name: PE
what: A trauma-focused behavioural therapy for PTSD. Instead of avoiding memories and reminders of the trauma, the person repeatedly revisits the memory in detail with the therapist and gradually approaches safe situations they have been avoiding. Over time this reduces fear and helps the trauma be processed and understood differently.
origin: Developed by Edna Foa and colleagues in the United States during the 1980s, initially with rape survivors, based on emotional processing theory; first trial results published in 1991.
evidence: Many randomised trials, including with veterans and assault survivors, show prolonged exposure reduces PTSD symptoms substantially, with effects similar to other trauma-focused therapies. Dropout can be notable.
practice: Individual, usually 8 to 15 weekly sessions of 90 minutes; intensive versions exist. Sessions include breathing retraining, recounting the trauma aloud (recorded to listen to at home), and real-life exposure tasks. Delivered by psychologists and trained trauma therapists.
suitability: Used for PTSD in adults, including military and assault-related trauma. NICE includes prolonged exposure among types of trauma-focused CBT for adults with PTSD (NG116). It may not suit people who are not yet stable or safe.
cautions: Symptoms can temporarily worsen as trauma is revisited; it requires trained delivery.
uk: Available in some NHS trauma and veterans' services and NHS Talking Therapies, and from private trauma-trained psychologists and BABCP-accredited therapists.

name: TF-CBT
aka: Trauma-focused CBT; in the UK also a broad umbrella term for several trauma-focused CBT types
what: CBT adapted for people who have experienced trauma. The best-known manualised model is for children and young people with a caregiver, covering skills for managing feelings, a gradual 'trauma narrative' and safety. In UK guidance, trauma-focused CBT is also used more broadly to include CPT, prolonged exposure and cognitive therapy for PTSD.
origin: The manualised child model was developed by Judith Cohen, Anthony Mannarino and Esther Deblinger in the United States during the 1990s. Adult trauma-focused CBT approaches, including cognitive therapy for PTSD by Anke Ehlers and David Clark, developed alongside in the UK.
evidence: Many randomised trials show trauma-focused CBT reduces PTSD symptoms in children, young people and adults. It is among the best-supported treatments for PTSD.
practice: Individual, often with caregiver sessions for children; typically 8 to 20 weekly sessions of about an hour. Work includes education about trauma, relaxation and coping skills, recounting the trauma, changing unhelpful beliefs and planning safety. Delivered by psychologists and trained therapists.
suitability: Used for PTSD and trauma symptoms. NICE recommends trauma-focused CBT for children, young people and adults with PTSD (NG116). It may need adapting for people with ongoing danger or severe instability.
cautions: Talking about trauma can temporarily increase distress; delivery should be by trained clinicians.
uk: Available through NHS child and adolescent mental health services, NHS Talking Therapies and trauma services, and privately from BABCP-accredited therapists and clinical psychologists.
checkNotes: Founding year approximate; 'TF-CBT' refers both to the Cohen-Mannarino-Deblinger child model and to the wider UK umbrella term, entry covers both.

name: NET
aka: KidNET is a version for children
what: A short-term trauma therapy for people who have lived through many traumatic events, such as war, torture or displacement. With the therapist, the person tells their whole life story in order, slowing down to process the worst events in detail, while also marking positive moments. A written biography is produced and given to them.
origin: Developed by Maggie Schauer, Frank Neuner and Thomas Elbert, of the University of Konstanz and the NGO vivo, in the early 2000s, first with refugees in Uganda.
evidence: Multiple randomised trials, many in low-resource and refugee settings, show narrative exposure therapy reduces PTSD symptoms after multiple traumas. Some trials are small or from the developers' group, and effects compared with other active treatments are less clear.
practice: Individual, usually 4 to 12 sessions of 90 to 120 minutes. You lay out a 'lifeline' with stones and flowers for bad and good events, then narrate events chronologically while the therapist helps you stay with emotions and sensations. Delivered by trained clinicians and, in some settings, trained lay counsellors.
suitability: Used for PTSD after multiple or prolonged trauma, including refugees and survivors of conflict. NICE lists narrative exposure therapy among types of trauma-focused CBT for adults with PTSD (NG116).
cautions: Revisiting traumatic events can be temporarily distressing; ongoing danger or insecure legal status may need addressing alongside.
uk: Offered by some NHS trauma services and charities working with refugees and asylum seekers; limited availability privately.
checkNotes: Exact founding year approximate (first trial c. 2004; manual 2005).

name: BSP
what: A therapy, developed from EMDR, in which the therapist helps a person find an eye position, a 'brainspot', that seems linked to a strong emotional or bodily response while thinking about a difficult experience. The person keeps their gaze there while noticing what comes up. Practitioners claim this helps process trauma held below conscious awareness.
origin: Developed by American psychotherapist David Grand, an EMDR practitioner, in New York around 2003.
evidence: Evidence is limited to a few small studies, often by people linked to the method or without strong controls. Its proposed mechanism, that eye position gives access to specific stored trauma, has not been tested. It is not recommended in NICE guidance.
practice: Individual, usually 50 to 90 minute sessions, with number not fixed. The therapist uses a pointer to guide your gaze, sometimes with headphones playing alternating sounds, while you attend quietly to feelings and sensations. Delivered by therapists who have done brainspotting training workshops.
suitability: Promoted for trauma, anxiety and performance issues, but without good evidence for any specific condition. Evidence-based treatments for PTSD, such as trauma-focused CBT or EMDR, have much stronger support.
cautions: Training is offered commercially and not independently regulated; check the therapist's core professional registration. Can be emotionally intense.
uk: Available only privately from therapists with brainspotting training; check they are on an HCPC or PSA-accredited register such as BACP or UKCP. Not offered in the NHS.

name: ART
what: A brief trauma therapy that combines eye movements, similar to EMDR, with imaginal exposure and 'voluntary image replacement'. The person recalls a distressing memory, then mentally rehearses replacing the troubling images with new ones of their choosing, while keeping the facts of what happened. It aims to reduce distress in few sessions.
origin: Developed by American therapist Laney Rosenzweig in 2008, drawing on EMDR and other techniques; research led from the University of South Florida.
evidence: A small number of trials, mainly with US veterans and from one research group, report reduced PTSD symptoms within a few sessions. The evidence is promising but early, with few independent replications. It is not in NICE guidance.
practice: Individual, typically 1 to 5 sessions of around an hour. You recall the memory and bodily sensations while following the therapist's hand with your eyes, then use guided imagery to rescript it. Delivered by licensed clinicians trained in ART.
suitability: Mainly studied for PTSD in veterans and service members, also used for anxiety and grief. Treatments with stronger evidence for PTSD are available.
cautions: Few UK practitioners; check the therapist's core professional registration as ART training itself is not regulated.
uk: Rarely available; only from a small number of private practitioners trained through ART International. Not offered in the NHS.

name: IFS
aka: Internal Family Systems model; IFS therapy
what: A therapy based on the idea that the mind is made up of many 'parts', such as protective managers, reactive firefighters and wounded exiles, along with a calm core 'Self'. The therapist helps the person get to know and understand their parts with curiosity and compassion, so that burdens from painful experiences can be released.
origin: Developed by American family therapist Richard C. Schwartz in the 1980s, applying ideas from family systems therapy to people's inner lives; his main book was published in 1995.
evidence: Research is limited: a small randomised trial in rheumatoid arthritis and small uncontrolled studies in depression and PTSD report benefits. There are no large trials and it is not in NICE guidance. Its popularity has grown faster than its evidence.
practice: Usually individual, sometimes couples or groups; weekly sessions of about an hour, often over months. You turn attention inward, notice parts as feelings, thoughts or sensations, and dialogue with them, guided by the therapist. Delivered by therapists trained through the IFS Institute or other programmes.
suitability: Used for trauma, anxiety, depression, relationship difficulties and self-criticism. Evidence-based trauma therapies have stronger support for PTSD. Care is needed for people with severe dissociation or complex trauma.
cautions: Work with 'exiled' parts can bring up intense trauma material; choose an experienced, appropriately registered therapist. Training is not regulated.
uk: Mainly private practitioners with IFS training; check membership of an HCPC or PSA-accredited register such as BACP or UKCP. Not routinely offered in the NHS.

name: STAIR
display: Skills Training in Affective and Interpersonal Regulation (STAIR)
aka: Often combined with narrative therapy as STAIR Narrative Therapy
what: A skills-based trauma therapy for people whose trauma, often in childhood, has left them struggling to manage emotions and relationships. It first builds skills in recognising and regulating feelings and in relating to others, and is often followed by a phase of telling and processing the trauma story.
origin: Developed by Marylene Cloitre and colleagues in New York in the late 1990s; first trial published in 2002.
evidence: Several randomised trials, including with women who experienced childhood abuse and with veterans, show STAIR, especially followed by trauma narrative work, reduces PTSD symptoms and improves emotional regulation. Trials are moderate in number and size.
practice: Individual or group, usually about 8 to 10 skills sessions, followed in the combined version by about 8 narrative sessions; also offered online in some services. Sessions teach and practise emotion and relationship skills. Delivered by psychologists and trained trauma therapists.
suitability: Used for PTSD and complex PTSD after childhood or repeated trauma, and for veterans. It is not specifically named in NICE guidance.
uk: Limited availability; occasionally in NHS trauma services and privately from trauma-trained psychologists.
checkNotes: NICE NG116 mentions phased approaches with stabilisation for complex PTSD but I did not confirm whether STAIR is named; entry says it is not specifically named. UK availability poorly documented.

name: Mentalization-Based
familyNote: The source does not state its family; MBT grew from psychoanalytic and attachment theory, so it is placed in psychodynamic and analytic.
what: A psychotherapy that helps people improve 'mentalising': the ability to make sense of their own and others' thoughts, feelings and intentions, especially under emotional stress. Difficulties in mentalising are thought to drive the unstable relationships and impulsive actions seen in borderline personality disorder.
origin: Developed by Anthony Bateman and Peter Fonagy in London, at St Ann's Hospital and University College London, in the 1990s; first randomised trial published in 1999.
evidence: Several randomised trials show MBT reduces self-harm, suicide attempts and hospital admission in borderline personality disorder, with some long-term follow-up. Evidence for adolescents and other conditions is more mixed.
practice: Usually combines weekly individual and group sessions over 12 to 18 months, often in a day-hospital or community setting. The therapist takes a curious, 'not-knowing' stance, slowing down to explore what people were feeling and thinking in recent interactions. Delivered by trained mental health teams.
suitability: Mainly used for borderline personality disorder and self-harm; adapted versions exist for adolescents, families and antisocial personality disorder. It is demanding and requires commitment over a long period.
uk: Offered by some NHS personality disorder and community mental health services; limited private availability through trained therapists, often on HCPC or UKCP registers.
checkNotes: NICE BPD guidance (CG78) does not specifically recommend MBT, so NICE is not mentioned. Family chosen as pd; could also be considered integrative.

name: Psychoanalysis
what: An intensive talking treatment in which the person speaks as freely as possible, often lying on a couch, several times a week. The idea is that unconscious feelings, memories and conflicts shape present difficulties, and that understanding them, including through the relationship with the analyst, brings lasting change.
origin: Developed by Sigmund Freud in Vienna in the 1890s, building on work with Josef Breuer; Freud first used the term psychoanalysis in 1896.
evidence: Research on full psychoanalysis is limited: few randomised trials exist because treatment is long and intensive. Some naturalistic studies and a small number of trials of long-term psychoanalytic therapy suggest benefit for long-standing depression and personality difficulties, but the evidence is weaker than for shorter structured therapies.
practice: Individual sessions of about 50 minutes, typically three to five times a week for several years. You say whatever comes to mind; the analyst listens, says relatively little, and offers interpretations. Delivered by trained psychoanalysts, mostly in private practice.
suitability: Usually sought for long-standing emotional, relationship or personality difficulties by people wanting deep self-understanding and able to commit time and money. Less suited to people needing quick symptom relief, in acute crisis, or with active psychosis.
cautions: Very costly and time-consuming. Psychoanalyst is not a protected title in the UK; checking registration with an accredited register is advisable.
uk: Mainly private; low-fee schemes exist through some training institutes. Practitioners may be on the British Psychoanalytic Council register. Rarely available on the NHS.

name: Psychodynamic
what: A talking therapy derived from psychoanalysis but usually less intensive. It explores how past experiences, unconscious patterns and recurring ways of relating to others shape current feelings and problems, using the relationship with the therapist as a window onto those patterns.
origin: Grew out of Freud's psychoanalysis as later analysts adapted it for once- or twice-weekly face-to-face work, from roughly the 1920s to the 1950s in Europe, Britain and the United States.
evidence: Meta-analyses of randomised trials show psychodynamic therapy helps depression and some anxiety and personality problems, often with effects similar to other bona fide therapies, though trials are fewer than for CBT. Short-term forms have the strongest evidence; evidence for open-ended long-term therapy is more limited.
practice: Usually individual 50-minute sessions once or twice a week, lasting from a few months to several years; group forms exist. Conversation is relatively unstructured: you talk about what matters to you and the therapist helps you notice patterns. Delivered by psychotherapists and some counsellors and psychologists.
suitability: Used for depression, anxiety, relationship difficulties and long-standing emotional problems, particularly for people interested in understanding the roots of their difficulties. NICE includes short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy among treatment options for depression. May not suit people wanting structured skills-based work.
cautions: Psychotherapists are not statutorily regulated in the UK; check membership of an accredited register.
uk: NHS psychotherapy services (often with long waits), short-term forms through some NHS Talking Therapies services, and private therapists on BPC, UKCP or BACP registers.
checkNotes: Founding year 1940 is a rough convention for the emergence of psychodynamic psychotherapy as distinct from psychoanalysis; there is no single founding date.

name: Jungian Analysis
what: A depth therapy based on Carl Jung's ideas that the psyche includes a personal and a collective unconscious, and that people move towards wholeness, which Jung called individuation. Work often includes dreams, images, symbols and creative expression alongside talking.
origin: Developed by Carl Gustav Jung in Zurich, Switzerland, after his break with Freud in 1913; he called his approach analytical psychology.
evidence: There are very few controlled trials. Some naturalistic and outcome studies, mainly from German-speaking countries, report improvements, but the evidence base is small and of limited quality, and Jung's broader concepts are difficult to test scientifically.
practice: Individual sessions of about 50 minutes, often one to three times a week over months or years. You talk about your life and inner experience, frequently bring dreams, and may use drawing, sandplay or active imagination. Delivered by Jungian analysts or Jungian-oriented psychotherapists.
suitability: Often sought by adults interested in meaning, personal development, midlife transitions or spiritual questions, as well as emotional difficulties. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. Less suited to people wanting brief, structured symptom-focused help.
cautions: Mostly private and long term, so costly. Check that a practitioner is registered with an accredited register.
uk: Mainly private practice; analysts trained by UK Jungian societies may be registered with the British Psychoanalytic Council or UKCP. Very limited NHS availability.

name: Adlerian Therapy
what: An approach based on Alfred Adler's individual psychology, which sees people as goal-directed and social, shaped by feelings of inferiority and a striving to belong and contribute. Therapy explores a person's lifestyle and early memories, challenges mistaken beliefs and encourages social interest.
origin: Developed by Alfred Adler in Vienna after he left Freud's circle in 1911; he named his approach individual psychology around 1912.
evidence: Research is limited: mostly small studies, case reports and evaluations of Adlerian-based parenting programmes. There is little high-quality trial evidence for Adlerian psychotherapy itself, though Adler's ideas influenced later approaches including cognitive therapies.
practice: Individual, couple, family or group sessions; often more structured and educational than classical analysis, with exploration of family background, birth order and early memories, then encouragement towards new behaviour. Length varies from brief to longer term. Delivered by counsellors and psychotherapists trained in the approach.
suitability: Used for personal, relationship and parenting difficulties, and in schools and family education. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. People seeking an approach with strong trial evidence for a specific disorder may prefer others.
uk: Small number of private practitioners and training through Adlerian organisations in the UK; occasionally available through counselling services. Not routinely offered on the NHS.

name: Object Relations
aka: Object relations psychotherapy; British object relations school
what: A psychodynamic approach focused on how early relationships, especially with caregivers, become internal templates (internal objects) that shape how we relate to ourselves and others. Therapy pays close attention to the relationship with the therapist, where these patterns tend to reappear and can be understood.
origin: Developed mainly in Britain from the 1930s to 1950s by Melanie Klein, Ronald Fairbairn, Donald Winnicott, Michael Balint and others; Fairbairn formulated an explicit object relations theory in the 1940s.
evidence: Object relations ideas underpin much psychodynamic therapy, but there are few trials of object relations therapy as a distinct method. Transference-focused psychotherapy, which draws on object relations theory, has some randomised-trial support for borderline personality disorder.
practice: Usually individual sessions once to several times a week, often over a long period; also applied to couples and groups. Conversation is open, with the therapist commenting on feelings and patterns arising in the room. Delivered by psychoanalytic psychotherapists.
suitability: Used for long-standing relationship difficulties, depression and personality problems, for people interested in exploring early experience. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance as a named therapy. May not suit those wanting short, structured treatment.
cautions: Long-term and often costly; check practitioners are on an accredited register.
uk: NHS psychotherapy departments in some areas, the Tavistock and Portman NHS tradition, and private psychotherapists registered with the BPC or UKCP.
checkNotes: Year 1940 is approximate; the school developed over the 1930s to 1950s.

name: Self Psychology
what: A psychoanalytic approach centred on the development of a cohesive sense of self. It proposes that people need empathic responses from others (selfobjects) to build self-esteem, and that therapy helps through the therapist's sustained empathy and by working through moments when that empathy fails.
origin: Developed by the Austrian-American psychoanalyst Heinz Kohut in Chicago, beginning with his book The Analysis of the Self in 1971.
evidence: There is very little controlled research on self psychology as a distinct therapy. Its ideas about empathy and the therapeutic relationship are consistent with research on common factors, but specific outcome evidence is limited to case studies and small studies.
practice: Individual sessions, often once or more a week over a long period. The therapist works to understand your experience from your point of view, with particular attention to self-esteem, shame and feeling understood. Delivered by psychoanalysts and psychodynamic psychotherapists.
suitability: Historically associated with narcissistic difficulties, fragile self-esteem and shame-related problems. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. May not suit people wanting brief, structured help.
uk: Mostly through private psychoanalytic psychotherapists who incorporate self psychology; registered practitioners can be found via the BPC or UKCP. Rarely offered as a named NHS treatment.

name: Lacanian Analysis
what: A form of psychoanalysis based on Jacques Lacan's rereading of Freud, which emphasises language, desire and how the unconscious is 'structured like a language'. The analyst attends closely to the person's words and slips, and may end sessions at variable points to highlight what has been said.
origin: Developed by the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan in Paris from the early 1950s; his 1953 Rome discourse launched his 'return to Freud'.
evidence: There is very little systematic outcome research on Lacanian analysis, and its practitioners have often been sceptical of standardised measurement. Its effectiveness has not been established in controlled trials.
practice: Individual sessions, often more than once a week over years, using the couch at later stages. Session length can vary and may be short. You speak freely; the analyst says little and punctuates your speech. Delivered by analysts trained in Lacanian schools.
suitability: Sought mainly by adults interested in psychoanalytic exploration; widely practised in France, Latin America and parts of Europe, less so in the UK. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance.
cautions: Variable, sometimes very short sessions differ from usual UK practice; ask about the format and fees beforehand.
uk: A small number of private practitioners and Lacanian training organisations, mainly in London; some practitioners are on UKCP registers. Not available on the NHS.
checkNotes: Unsure exactly which UK registers Lacanian organisations currently belong to, so this is stated cautiously.

name: Brief Psychodynamic
aka: Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy (STPP); includes dynamic interpersonal therapy (DIT) and intensive short-term dynamic psychotherapy (ISTDP)
what: Time-limited versions of psychodynamic therapy that agree a central focus, such as a recurring relationship pattern linked to current symptoms, and work on it actively within a fixed number of sessions. The therapist is usually more active than in open-ended therapy.
origin: Developed from the 1960s by David Malan at the Tavistock Clinic in London, Peter Sifneos and James Mann in Boston, and Habib Davanloo in Montreal; Malan's A Study of Brief Psychotherapy appeared in 1963.
evidence: Meta-analyses of randomised trials show short-term psychodynamic therapy is effective for depression and some anxiety and somatic problems, often comparable to other therapies. NICE includes it among treatment options for adults with depression and lists focal psychodynamic therapy as an option for adults with anorexia nervosa.
practice: Individual weekly sessions of about 50 minutes, typically 8 to 30 sessions. After agreeing a focus, you and the therapist explore feelings and relationship patterns linked to it, including how they show up in therapy. Delivered by psychotherapists, psychologists and trained NHS practitioners.
suitability: Used for depression, some anxiety problems and relationship-linked difficulties. NICE guidance for depression includes short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy as an option, and NICE eating-disorder guidance includes focal psychodynamic therapy for adult anorexia. May not suit people in crisis needing a different service.
cautions: Psychotherapists are not statutorily regulated in the UK; check registration with an accredited register.
uk: Available in some NHS Talking Therapies services (often as dynamic interpersonal therapy), NHS psychotherapy departments, and private practitioners registered with the BPC, UKCP or BACP.
checkNotes: NICE NG222 lists short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy in its tables of treatment options for depression (less and more severe), but not as a first choice; exact wording not re-checked. Focal psychodynamic therapy for adult anorexia in NG69 recalled rather than freshly verified. DIT availability varies by NHS Talking Therapies service.

name: Person-Centered
aka: Client-centred therapy; Rogerian therapy; person-centred counselling
what: A humanistic talking therapy that trusts people's own capacity to grow when given the right relationship. The therapist offers empathy, unconditional positive regard and genuineness, and follows the client's lead rather than directing, diagnosing or advising.
origin: Developed by the American psychologist Carl Rogers in the 1940s, first set out in Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942) and later named client-centred therapy.
evidence: Trials and meta-analyses suggest person-centred and related experiential therapies help depression and general distress, with effects broadly similar to other therapies in some comparisons, though trials are fewer and quality varies. NICE includes counselling among treatment options for depression.
practice: Usually individual weekly 50-minute sessions, from around six sessions to open-ended; also used in groups. You decide what to talk about; the counsellor listens closely and reflects back your feelings and meanings rather than giving advice. Delivered by counsellors and psychotherapists.
suitability: Widely used for depression, stress, bereavement and life difficulties. NICE depression guidance includes counselling as an option, and NHS Talking Therapies offer counselling for depression, which draws on person-centred and emotion-focused methods. May suit less well those wanting structured, directive techniques.
cautions: Counsellors are not statutorily regulated in the UK; check membership of an accredited register such as BACP or UKCP.
uk: Counselling for depression via NHS Talking Therapies, GP-attached and workplace counselling, voluntary sector services, and private counsellors on BACP, UKCP or NCPS registers.

name: Gestalt
what: A humanistic, experiential therapy that focuses on present-moment awareness: what you are feeling, thinking and doing right now, including in your body and in contact with the therapist. Experiments, such as speaking to an imagined person in an empty chair, help bring unfinished feelings into awareness.
origin: Developed by Fritz Perls, Laura Perls and Paul Goodman in New York; the founding book, Gestalt Therapy, was published in 1951.
evidence: Evidence is limited: some small trials and naturalistic studies show improvements, and chair-work techniques have support within emotion-focused therapy research. There are few large, high-quality trials of Gestalt therapy itself.
practice: Individual or group sessions, often weekly for months. Sessions are active: the therapist may draw attention to your posture or tone, or suggest experiments such as empty-chair dialogue or role-play. Delivered by Gestalt psychotherapists and counsellors.
suitability: Used for anxiety, depression, relationship difficulties and personal development, especially by people open to experiential work. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. Intense experiential exercises may not suit people who are very fragile or in crisis.
cautions: Emotionally intense techniques should be used carefully with people who have trauma histories. Check that the practitioner is on an accredited register.
uk: Mainly private Gestalt psychotherapists and counsellors registered with UKCP or BACP; some voluntary sector services. Rarely offered as a named NHS treatment.

name: Existential
what: A philosophical approach to therapy that helps people face basic conditions of life, such as freedom, choice, meaning, isolation and death, and explore how they live in relation to them. It aims to clarify a person's own values and way of being rather than to cure symptoms.
origin: Rooted in European existential philosophy; developed by Ludwig Binswanger and Medard Boss in Switzerland from the 1940s, Rollo May and Irvin Yalom in the US, and Emmy van Deurzen in Britain from the 1970s.
evidence: Research is limited. Meaning-centred and existential interventions show promising results in trials with people facing serious illness, but there are few trials of existential psychotherapy more generally.
practice: Usually individual weekly sessions; also groups. Conversation is open and philosophical, focusing on your lived experience, choices and what gives your life meaning. The therapist is engaged and questioning rather than technique-driven. Delivered by existential psychotherapists and counsellors.
suitability: Often sought around life crises, loss, illness, midlife questions and loss of meaning. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. May not suit people wanting a structured, symptom-focused programme.
uk: Mainly private practitioners trained in existential approaches and registered with UKCP or BACP; some training institutes offer low-cost clinics. Not routinely available on the NHS.
checkNotes: Year 1958 (Rollo May's edited book Existence) is a conventional marker; existential therapy has no single founding date.

name: Logotherapy
what: An approach developed by Viktor Frankl that holds the search for meaning to be a primary human motivation. Therapy helps people find meaning even in unavoidable suffering, using techniques such as paradoxical intention and shifting attention away from oneself.
origin: Developed by the Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl in Vienna from the late 1920s and 1930s; it became widely known through his 1946 book on his experience of Nazi concentration camps, later titled Man's Search for Meaning.
evidence: Evidence is limited, mostly small studies of mixed quality. Some meaning-centred interventions influenced by Frankl have shown benefit in trials with people with advanced cancer, but logotherapy itself has little high-quality trial evidence.
practice: Usually individual sessions, sometimes groups, often relatively brief. Conversation explores values, responsibility and sources of meaning; the therapist may use Socratic questioning or paradoxical intention for fears. Delivered by trained psychotherapists and counsellors.
suitability: Used for loss of meaning, grief, illness, and existential distress. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. People wanting a treatment with strong evidence for a specific disorder may prefer others.
uk: Very few UK practitioners specialise in logotherapy; it is mainly available privately, sometimes integrated by existential therapists registered with UKCP or BACP. Not offered on the NHS.
checkNotes: Founding year uncertain: Frankl used the term in the 1920s or 1930s; 1938 is a commonly cited date for its first published use.

name: Focusing
what: A practice of paying gentle attention to a vague, bodily-felt sense of a situation (a 'felt sense') and letting words or images emerge from it. It is used on its own as a self-help skill or within therapy to help people move forward with feelings that are hard to put into words.
origin: Developed by the philosopher and psychologist Eugene Gendlin at the University of Chicago, working with Carl Rogers, from research on therapy outcomes in the 1960s; popularised by his 1978 book Focusing.
evidence: Studies link clients' depth of experiencing with better outcomes in several therapies, and some small trials of focusing show benefits, but the evidence for focusing as a standalone treatment is limited and of modest quality.
practice: Can be taught individually or in groups, or used with a partner who listens. Sessions involve pausing, noticing the body's felt sense of an issue and checking which words fit. Delivered by focusing trainers and focusing-oriented therapists.
suitability: Used for personal growth, stress, and alongside therapy for people who find feelings hard to name. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. Not a substitute for treatment of severe mental illness.
cautions: Focusing trainers are not regulated; credentials vary.
uk: Private focusing teachers and focusing-oriented therapists, some registered with BACP or UKCP; UK focusing organisations run courses. Not offered on the NHS.

name: Emotion-Focused
aka: Emotion-focused therapy for individuals; formerly process-experiential therapy. Not to be confused with emotionally focused couple therapy or Emotional Freedom Techniques
what: An evidence-based humanistic therapy that treats emotions as central to change. Within an empathic relationship, the therapist helps people access, understand and transform painful emotions, for example through chair dialogues with a critical part of oneself or with someone from the past.
origin: Developed by Leslie Greenberg with Laura Rice and Robert Elliott, mainly at York University, Toronto, from the 1980s; the name emotion-focused therapy replaced process-experiential therapy in the early 2000s.
evidence: Randomised trials show emotion-focused therapy helps depression, with results similar to CBT in some trials, and there is growing evidence for complex trauma and social anxiety. Trials are fewer and smaller than for CBT, and it is not named in NICE guidance.
practice: Usually individual weekly sessions, often 16 to 20 for depression. Alongside empathic conversation, the therapist guides tasks such as two-chair or empty-chair work and focusing on bodily feelings. Delivered by psychotherapists, psychologists and counsellors with EFT training.
suitability: Used for depression, trauma, anxiety and emotional difficulties. It informs counselling for depression in NHS Talking Therapies. Not named in NICE guidance. Intense emotional work may need adapting for people in crisis.
cautions: Check practitioners have specific EFT training and are on an accredited register.
uk: Mainly private practitioners on UKCP, BACP or HCPC registers; elements appear in NHS Talking Therapies counselling for depression.
checkNotes: Year 2002 refers to the adoption of the name emotion-focused therapy (Greenberg's book of that year); the approach dates to the 1980s and 1990s as process-experiential therapy.

name: Process-Experiential
aka: Process-experiential emotion-focused therapy (PE-EFT); earlier name for emotion-focused therapy
what: A humanistic therapy combining a person-centred relationship with active, emotion-focused tasks chosen when specific 'markers' appear in a session, such as self-criticism or unresolved feelings towards someone. It is the earlier name and form of emotion-focused therapy.
origin: Developed by Leslie Greenberg, Laura Rice and Robert Elliott in Canada and the US during the 1980s, set out in their 1993 book Facilitating Emotional Change.
evidence: Randomised trials in the 1990s and 2000s, notably for depression, found process-experiential therapy at least as effective as person-centred therapy and comparable to CBT. Evidence is moderate but based on relatively few trials.
practice: Individual weekly sessions, often 16 to 20. The therapist listens empathically and, when a relevant marker emerges, suggests a task such as two-chair dialogue, empty-chair work or focusing. Delivered by trained psychotherapists and counsellors.
suitability: Used for depression and emotional difficulties linked to self-criticism or unresolved relationships. Not named in NICE guidance. Today usually practised under the name emotion-focused therapy.
uk: Usually offered as emotion-focused therapy by private practitioners on UKCP, BACP or HCPC registers; influences NHS Talking Therapies counselling for depression.
checkNotes: Status as a distinct therapy is debatable since the term is now largely superseded by emotion-focused therapy.

name: Transactional Analysis
what: A therapy and theory of personality and communication that describes three 'ego states' (Parent, Adult, Child), the transactions between people, repeated 'games' and unconscious 'life scripts'. Therapy helps people recognise these patterns and make new decisions about how to live and relate.
origin: Developed by the Canadian-born psychiatrist Eric Berne in California in the late 1950s; first described in papers from 1958 and popularised by Games People Play (1964).
evidence: Evidence is limited: mostly small studies, practice-based evaluations and case studies. There are few high-quality randomised trials of TA psychotherapy for specific mental health problems.
practice: Individual, couple or group sessions, often weekly; may be short or long term. Uses diagrams and plain-language concepts, and the client and therapist agree an explicit contract for change. Delivered by TA psychotherapists and counsellors; also used in education and organisations.
suitability: Used for relationship and communication difficulties, personal development and a range of emotional problems. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. Those seeking a treatment with strong trial evidence for a specific disorder may prefer others.
uk: Mainly private TA psychotherapists and counsellors, many registered with UKCP or BACP through UK TA training organisations. Not routinely offered on the NHS.

name: Family Systems
aka: Systemic family therapy; family systems therapy. Read here as family therapy in general, not Internal Family Systems (IFS) or specifically Bowen's family systems theory
what: An approach that treats problems as arising within relationships and patterns of interaction, rather than solely inside one person. The therapist works with family members together to understand these patterns, improve communication and find new ways of responding to difficulties.
origin: Emerged in the United States in the 1950s through Gregory Bateson, Don Jackson, Nathan Ackerman, Murray Bowen, Virginia Satir and others, drawing on systems theory and cybernetics.
evidence: Systematic reviews and trials support family-based interventions for several problems, including eating disorders in young people, adolescent conduct and drug problems, and psychosis. NICE recommends eating-disorder-focused family therapy for children and young people with anorexia and family intervention for people with psychosis or schizophrenia.
practice: Sessions with the family or selected members, typically 60 to 90 minutes, every one to four weeks over several months. Sometimes a team observes and offers reflections. Delivered by family and systemic psychotherapists, often in NHS child and adolescent services.
suitability: Used for child and adolescent difficulties, eating disorders, psychosis, family conflict and adjustment to illness. NICE recommends family therapy for anorexia in young people and family intervention in psychosis. May be unsuitable where there is ongoing domestic abuse without safety measures.
cautions: Joint sessions may be unsafe where there is domestic abuse; services should screen for this. Family therapists are not statutorily regulated; check registration with UKCP or AFT.
uk: NHS child and adolescent mental health services, eating disorder and psychosis services, and private family and systemic psychotherapists via the Association for Family Therapy or UKCP.
checkNotes: 'Family Systems' is ambiguous: it could mean Bowen family systems theory (covered under Bowenian) or be confused with Internal Family Systems (IFS); interpreted as systemic family therapy in general. Year 1956 (Bateson group's double-bind paper) is a conventional marker.

name: Structural Family
what: A family therapy that looks at the structure of a family: its hierarchy, boundaries and alliances. The therapist joins the family and actively helps reorganise unhelpful patterns, for example by strengthening parents' ability to work together or clarifying boundaries between generations.
origin: Developed by Salvador Minuchin and colleagues in the 1960s at the Wiltwyck School in New York and later the Philadelphia Child Guidance Clinic; set out in Families and Family Therapy (1974).
evidence: Structural ideas strongly influenced family-based treatment for adolescent anorexia, which has good trial support, and brief strategic family therapy for adolescent behaviour problems. Trials of structural family therapy as a standalone named method are fewer, so its own evidence is moderate.
practice: Family sessions, often weekly or fortnightly for several months, usually around an hour. The therapist is active: observing interactions, asking family members to talk to each other in session (enactments) and setting tasks. Delivered by family therapists.
suitability: Used for child and adolescent behaviour problems, eating disorders and family conflict. NICE does not recommend structural family therapy by name, though its ideas inform recommended family therapy for anorexia in young people. Requires caution where there is family violence.
cautions: Directive interventions need to be safe and culturally sensitive; screen for domestic abuse before joint sessions.
uk: NHS child and adolescent mental health services and private family therapists registered with the Association for Family Therapy or UKCP, often within an integrative systemic approach.
checkNotes: Year 1974 is the key book; the approach was developed through the 1960s. The extent to which family-based treatment for anorexia derives from structural therapy is a simplification.

name: Strategic Family
what: A brief, problem-focused family therapy in which the therapist designs specific strategies, often including directives or tasks between sessions, to interrupt the patterns that keep a problem going. It focuses on changing behaviour in the present rather than on insight.
origin: Developed from the 1960s by Jay Haley and Cloé Madanes, building on work at the Mental Research Institute in Palo Alto with Gregory Bateson and on the methods of Milton Erickson; Haley's Strategies of Psychotherapy appeared in 1963.
evidence: Classic strategic family therapy has limited direct trial evidence. A derivative, brief strategic family therapy, has several randomised trials for adolescent behaviour and substance-use problems with generally positive but mixed results.
practice: Family or couple sessions, usually brief, often fewer than 10 to 20, around an hour each. The therapist defines the problem clearly, gives directives or tasks to try at home, and sometimes uses reframing or paradoxical instructions. Delivered by family therapists.
suitability: Used for child and adolescent behaviour problems and family conflict. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. Paradoxical techniques may not suit families wanting a transparent, collaborative approach.
cautions: Some historical strategic techniques were criticised as manipulative; contemporary practice is more collaborative. Screen for domestic abuse before joint sessions.
uk: Usually as part of integrative systemic practice by NHS or private family therapists registered with the Association for Family Therapy or UKCP; rarely offered under this name.
checkNotes: Founding year uncertain; 1963 (Haley's book) is one marker, with Haley's Problem-Solving Therapy (1976) another. Evidence level reflects classic strategic therapy, not brief strategic family therapy.

name: Milan Systemic
aka: Milan approach; Milan school of family therapy
what: A family therapy approach that views problems as part of the beliefs and relationship patterns of a whole system. It introduced techniques such as hypothesising, circular questioning (asking each person about relationships between others) and therapist neutrality, often with a team observing behind a screen.
origin: Developed in Milan, Italy, by Mara Selvini Palazzoli, Luigi Boscolo, Gianfranco Cecchin and Giuliana Prata from 1971; their book Paradox and Counterparadox appeared in 1975.
evidence: There is limited outcome research on the Milan approach itself, mostly small or uncontrolled studies. It has been highly influential, particularly in UK systemic training and practice, but its specific effectiveness has not been established in large trials.
practice: Family sessions, traditionally spaced about a month apart over around ten sessions. A therapist talks with the family while colleagues observe, then the team may offer reflections or an intervention. Delivered by family and systemic psychotherapists.
suitability: Used for a range of family difficulties and as a framework within broader systemic therapy. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance by name. May not suit families uncomfortable with observation by a team.
cautions: Families should be told and consent when a team or recording is used.
uk: Mainly through NHS child and adolescent services and family therapy clinics using systemic methods, and private systemic psychotherapists registered with the Association for Family Therapy or UKCP.
checkNotes: Year could be given as 1971 (team formed) or 1975 (book); 1975 chosen.

name: Bowenian
aka: Bowenian family therapy; Bowen theory; family systems theory (Bowen)
what: A family therapy based on Murray Bowen's theory that emotional patterns pass between generations. A core aim is 'differentiation of self': being able to stay emotionally connected to family while thinking and acting for oneself. Family trees (genograms) map patterns across generations.
origin: Developed by the American psychiatrist Murray Bowen from his research with families at the US National Institute of Mental Health in the 1950s and at Georgetown University from 1959; set out in papers from the 1960s.
evidence: Research is limited: some studies support links between differentiation and wellbeing, but there are very few controlled trials of Bowenian therapy as a treatment for mental health problems.
practice: Can be done with an individual, a couple or family members, often in weekly or less frequent sessions over months. The therapist is calm and coaching, helps build a genogram and encourages contact with the wider family to change patterns. Delivered by family therapists.
suitability: Used for family and couple conflict, and by people wanting to understand intergenerational patterns. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. People seeking a treatment for a specific diagnosis with strong evidence may prefer others.
uk: Few UK therapists practise Bowen therapy exclusively; genograms and Bowenian ideas are used by systemic family therapists in the NHS and privately (Association for Family Therapy or UKCP).
checkNotes: Year 1966 (Bowen's paper on family theory in clinical practice) is approximate.

name: EFT Couples
aka: Emotionally focused therapy for couples (EFCT); also used with families (EFFT). Not Emotional Freedom Techniques
what: A structured couple therapy grounded in attachment theory. It sees relationship distress as a cycle of negative interaction driven by unmet needs for closeness and security, and helps partners recognise the cycle, express underlying emotions and needs, and respond to each other in ways that rebuild a secure bond.
origin: Developed by Sue Johnson and Leslie Greenberg in Vancouver, Canada, in the early 1980s; first outcome study published in 1985.
evidence: Several randomised trials and meta-analyses show EFT improves relationship satisfaction for distressed couples, with fairly large effects, although many trials are small and conducted by developers. It is not specifically named in NICE guidance; NICE's couples recommendation for depression refers to behavioural couples therapy.
practice: Couple sessions, usually weekly for around 8 to 20 sessions of about 60 to 90 minutes. The therapist helps partners slow down arguments, notice the cycle and share softer feelings beneath anger or withdrawal. Delivered by couple therapists with EFT training.
suitability: Used for relationship distress, and sometimes where one partner has depression or trauma symptoms. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. Generally not suitable where there is ongoing violence or coercive control.
cautions: Couple therapy is generally not appropriate where there is current domestic abuse; services should screen for it. Check practitioners are on an accredited register.
uk: Mainly private couple therapists with EFT certification, often also registered with BACP, UKCP or COSRT. Not routinely offered as EFT on the NHS.
checkNotes: Exact first outcome study year (1985, Johnson and Greenberg) recalled rather than freshly verified.

name: Imago
what: A couple therapy proposing that people choose partners who resemble early caregivers (the 'imago'), and that conflict offers a chance to heal childhood wounds. Partners learn a structured way of talking, the Imago dialogue, in which one mirrors, validates and empathises with what the other says.
origin: Developed by Harville Hendrix and Helen LaKelly Hunt in the United States around 1980; popularised by Hendrix's book Getting the Love You Want (1988).
evidence: Evidence is limited: one published randomised trial found improved relationship satisfaction that was statistically but not clinically significant for most couples, alongside a few small studies. A larger trial has been completed but results were not found. Its theory of partner choice is largely untested.
practice: Couple sessions, often weekly for around 12 sessions, plus weekend workshops. You practise the structured Imago dialogue in session and at home with the therapist's coaching. Delivered by certified Imago therapists, often also qualified counsellors or psychotherapists.
suitability: Used for couples wanting better communication and less conflict. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. Not suitable where there is ongoing domestic abuse.
cautions: Couple work is generally not appropriate where there is current domestic abuse or coercive control. Imago certification is not a UK regulatory credential.
uk: Private Imago therapists and workshops; some are also registered with BACP or UKCP. Not offered on the NHS.
checkNotes: Founding year c.1980 is approximate. Results of the completed University of Pennsylvania Imago trial (NCT04302844) could not be found.

name: Solution-Focused Family
aka: Solution-focused brief therapy (SFBT) with families and couples
what: A brief, future-focused approach that spends little time on problems and more on what the family wants instead, times when things already go better, and the strengths they bring. Techniques include the 'miracle question' and scaling questions to identify small, achievable next steps.
origin: Developed by Steve de Shazer, Insoo Kim Berg and colleagues at the Brief Family Therapy Center in Milwaukee, USA, in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
evidence: Many studies and several meta-analyses report small to moderate benefits for a range of child, family and adult problems, but trials vary widely in quality and few are large. It is not specifically recommended in NICE guidance.
practice: Family, couple or individual sessions, typically few (often three to eight) and around an hour. The therapist asks questions about goals, exceptions and progress, and may suggest noticing what works between sessions. Delivered by family therapists, social workers, counsellors and school staff.
suitability: Used widely in child and family services, schools and social care for behaviour, family conflict and coping. Not specifically recommended in NICE guidance. May not suit severe or complex mental illness on its own.
cautions: Practitioners' training varies widely; the approach is used by many professions without specific accreditation.
uk: NHS child and family services, schools, social care and voluntary organisations, and private practitioners registered with UKCP, BACP or the Association for Family Therapy.
checkNotes: Evidence level could reasonably be rated limited rather than moderate given variable trial quality. Founding year approximate.

name: Somatic Experiencing
what: A body-focused approach to trauma and stress. It assumes that trauma can leave the nervous system stuck in a state of threat, and it helps people notice bodily sensations and gently release or complete stress responses a little at a time, rather than retelling the traumatic story in detail.
origin: Developed by Peter Levine in the United States from the 1970s, drawing on stress physiology and observations of animal responses to threat; popularised by his 1997 book Waking the Tiger.
evidence: Research is limited: one randomised trial in PTSD reported benefits, alongside small uncontrolled studies and reviews that call the evidence promising but low in quality. It is not one of the trauma therapies recommended in NICE guidance for PTSD, and its theoretical model has not been firmly established.
practice: Usually individual sessions of about an hour, weekly, for an open-ended number of sessions. A practitioner guides you to notice sensations, posture and small movements, moving between distressing and calming feelings at a slow pace. Some practitioners use light touch with consent. Practitioners complete a multi-year SE training on top of another background.
suitability: Commonly sought by people with trauma, chronic stress or anxiety who prefer a body-based approach or find talking about events overwhelming. It may not suit people wanting a structured, evidence-based PTSD treatment or those uncomfortable with attention to bodily sensations.
