cautions: The title is not regulated in the UK; training varies and some practitioners have no core mental-health qualification. Body work with trauma can stir strong feelings, so check a practitioner's background and registration.
uk: Mainly private practitioners; not routinely offered on the NHS. Look for therapists also registered with BACP, UKCP or HCPC.

name: Hakomi
aka: Hakomi Method; Hakomi mindful somatic psychotherapy
what: A body-centred psychotherapy that uses mindfulness to explore how habits, beliefs and early experiences show up in posture, gesture and tension. The therapist sets up small, gentle experiments in a calm, accepting atmosphere so that a person can notice and reconsider long-held patterns.
origin: Developed by Ron Kurtz in the United States in the 1970s, influenced by Buddhist and Taoist ideas, body psychotherapy and systems thinking; the Hakomi Institute was founded in 1981.
evidence: There is very little formal research: mainly case reports, practitioner accounts and small studies. No good-quality controlled trials show that it works for specific mental-health problems, and it does not appear in NICE guidance.
practice: Usually individual weekly sessions of about an hour, sometimes groups or workshops. You may be invited to slow down, attend to inner experience, and try a small experiment such as hearing a phrase or noticing a gesture, then explore what arises. Some touch may be used with consent.
suitability: Used by adults seeking a gentle, exploratory therapy for relationship patterns, low self-worth or emotional difficulties, often those drawn to mindfulness. It is not an established treatment for severe or acute mental illness.
cautions: Hakomi practitioner is not a protected title in the UK. Check whether the therapist is also on an accredited register.
uk: Available through private practitioners and Hakomi trainings; not offered on the NHS. Some practitioners are registered with UKCP or BACP.
checkNotes: Exact start year of Hakomi uncertain (mid-1970s); 1976 used as approximate.

name: Bioenergetics
what: A form of body psychotherapy that sees chronic muscular tension as a physical record of suppressed emotion and defensive character patterns. It combines talking with breathing, stress positions, grounding and expressive movements intended to release tension and increase emotional aliveness.
origin: Developed in New York by Alexander Lowen and John Pierrakos, students of Wilhelm Reich, who founded the Institute for Bioenergetic Analysis in 1956.
evidence: Evidence is limited to small uncontrolled studies, a few naturalistic outcome studies and clinical reports. There are no robust trials establishing benefit for specific conditions, and its theory of stored energy and character armour is not supported by mainstream science.
practice: Individual sessions of about an hour, weekly, often over months or years; also group exercise classes. Sessions mix conversation with exercises such as standing grounding postures, deep breathing, kicking or vocalising, and some therapist touch.
suitability: Sought by adults interested in the link between body and emotion, for example around stress or emotional numbness. Intense cathartic exercises may not suit people with trauma, dissociation, psychosis, heart problems or physical injuries.
cautions: Strong physical and emotional exercises can be overwhelming or physically demanding. The title is not regulated in the UK; check training and registration.
uk: Small number of private practitioners and training groups; not available on the NHS. Some practitioners are registered with UKCP.

name: Rolfing
what: A form of deep, hands-on manipulation of the body's connective tissue (fascia), aiming to improve posture, alignment and ease of movement. It is a bodywork method rather than a psychotherapy, although some people seek it for emotional as well as physical reasons.
origin: Developed by biochemist Ida Rolf in the United States from the 1950s onwards; the Rolf Institute of Structural Integration was established in Boulder, Colorado, in 1971.
evidence: Research is sparse and small-scale, mostly on posture, chronic pain or movement, with mixed and low-quality findings. There is no credible evidence that it treats mental-health conditions, and claims about releasing stored emotion are not supported.
practice: Typically a series of about ten individual sessions of 60 to 90 minutes, each working on different areas of the body. You lie, sit or stand while the practitioner applies firm, sometimes uncomfortable, pressure with hands and elbows. Delivered by certified Rolfers in private practice.
suitability: Used mainly by people interested in posture, movement or body awareness. It is not a treatment for mental illness. Deep pressure may not suit people with osteoporosis, blood-clotting problems, recent injury, some skin conditions, or trauma histories that make touch distressing.
cautions: Can be painful. Not regulated in the UK. Speak to a doctor first about medical conditions that might make deep tissue work unsafe.
uk: Private practitioners only; not available on the NHS and not statutorily regulated.
checkNotes: Exact founding year is approximate (method developed gradually from c.1950s).

name: Feldenkrais
what: A movement-learning method that uses slow, gentle, attention-focused movements to help people become aware of habitual patterns and find easier, more efficient ways of moving. It is an educational approach rather than a psychotherapy.
origin: Developed by Moshe Feldenkrais, a physicist, engineer and judo teacher, from the 1940s, first in Britain and then in Israel, where he taught it from the 1950s.
evidence: Small trials and reviews suggest possible benefits for balance in older adults and some aspects of movement and quality of life, but studies are small and of mixed quality. There is little evidence for effects on mental-health conditions.
practice: Group classes (Awareness Through Movement), usually 45 to 60 minutes, where a teacher talks you through slow movements, often lying on the floor; or individual hands-on sessions (Functional Integration). Taught by teachers who complete a multi-year training.
suitability: Used by people with pain, stiffness, balance problems or movement difficulties, musicians and dancers, and people interested in body awareness. It is not a treatment for mental illness and is not a substitute for medical care for injuries or neurological conditions.
cautions: Generally gentle and low risk. Not statutorily regulated in the UK.
uk: Private teachers and classes; the Feldenkrais Guild UK lists trained practitioners. Not usually available on the NHS.

name: Alexander Technique
what: A method of re-learning how to use the body in everyday activities, by noticing and stopping unhelpful habits of tension, especially in the head, neck and back. It is taught as a skill rather than given as a treatment.
origin: Developed by F. M. Alexander, an Australian actor, in the 1890s after he lost his voice when performing; he later taught in London from 1904.
evidence: A large UK randomised trial found that Alexander Technique lessons reduced disability from chronic back pain in the longer term, and there is some trial evidence for neck pain. Evidence for other conditions, including mental health, is limited.
practice: Usually one-to-one lessons of 30 to 45 minutes, often a course of 10 to 20 or more, sometimes group classes. A teacher uses light hand contact and spoken guidance while you sit, stand, walk or do everyday actions.
suitability: Most often used for long-term back and neck pain, posture, and by performers such as musicians and actors. It is not a treatment for mental illness, though some people use it to manage stress.
cautions: Low risk. Teachers are not statutorily regulated, but can join the voluntary Complementary and Natural Healthcare Council register.
uk: Private teachers; the Society of Teachers of the Alexander Technique (STAT) and CNHC list registered teachers. Rarely available on the NHS.

name: Sensorimotor
what: A body-oriented talking therapy for trauma and attachment difficulties. It works with bodily sensations, posture and movement alongside thoughts and emotions, aiming to help people stay within a tolerable range of arousal and build resources before working with traumatic memories.
origin: Developed by Pat Ogden in the United States, drawing on Hakomi and neuroscience; she founded what became the Sensorimotor Psychotherapy Institute in 1981.
evidence: Research is limited to small pilot studies and case series reporting improvements in trauma symptoms and body awareness. There are no large, high-quality trials, and it is not among the PTSD treatments recommended by NICE.
practice: Individual sessions of about 50 to 60 minutes, usually weekly, often over months. The therapist helps you track sensations and impulses to move, practise grounding, and explore small physical actions, in a phased approach. Delivered by trained psychotherapists or counsellors with additional certification.
suitability: Used for complex or developmental trauma, dissociation and attachment difficulties, especially by people who find purely verbal therapy hard. People wanting a NICE-recommended PTSD therapy may prefer trauma-focused CBT or EMDR.
cautions: Not a protected title in the UK. Trauma work can be destabilising if paced poorly; check the therapist's core training and registration.
uk: Private practitioners, some of whom are registered with BACP, UKCP or HCPC. Not routinely offered by the NHS.

name: Dance/Movement
what: A psychotherapy that uses movement and dance as a way of expressing and exploring feelings, relationships and experiences. Based on the idea that body and mind are linked, the therapist works with how a person moves as well as what they say. No dance skill is needed.
origin: Emerged in the United States in the 1940s, notably through Marian Chace's work in psychiatric hospitals; the American Dance Therapy Association formed in 1966. In the UK the professional association began in 1982.
evidence: Meta-analyses suggest small to moderate benefits for depression, anxiety and quality of life, but many trials are small and at risk of bias. NICE guidance on psychosis and schizophrenia in adults includes it among the arts therapies that can be considered, particularly for negative symptoms.
practice: Individual or group sessions, often 50 to 90 minutes, weekly, in NHS, schools, hospitals, care settings or private practice. Sessions may include warm-ups, free or structured movement, mirroring, props and talking about what came up. Delivered by therapists with a master's-level training.
suitability: Used with adults and children with depression, anxiety, psychosis, dementia, learning disabilities, autism and trauma, and with people who find words difficult. It may not suit people who are very uncomfortable with movement or being seen.
cautions: Unlike art, music and drama therapists, dance movement psychotherapists are not regulated by the HCPC. Check registration with ADMP UK and, where held, UKCP.
uk: Some NHS, education and charity services; mostly private. The Association for Dance Movement Psychotherapy UK (ADMP UK) keeps a professional register; some practitioners are also UKCP-registered.
checkNotes: Verified that ADMP UK runs its own register and is an organisational member of UKCP (PSA-accredited); I could not confirm that ADMP's own register is itself PSA-accredited, so I did not say so. UK association founding year (1982) and Chace start date (c.1942) from memory. NICE CG178 'consider arts therapies' wording confirmed in secondary sources only.

name: Body Psychotherapy
what: An umbrella term for psychotherapies that work with the body as well as the mind, holding that emotions and experiences are expressed in breathing, posture, movement and tension. Therapists combine talking with attention to sensation, breath, movement and sometimes touch.
origin: Rooted in the work of Wilhelm Reich in Vienna and Berlin in the 1920s and 1930s, later developed by many schools such as bioenergetics, biodynamic psychotherapy and Hakomi.
evidence: Evidence is limited and varied because it covers many different methods. Some small trials and reviews report benefits for depression, somatic symptoms and psychosis, but quality is generally low. NICE guidance on psychosis lists body psychotherapy among arts therapies that can be considered.
practice: Usually individual sessions of about 50 to 60 minutes, weekly, sometimes groups. You might talk, notice sensations, breathe, move, or work with posture; some therapists use touch with explicit consent. Delivered by trained psychotherapists in private practice.
suitability: Used by adults with anxiety, depression, trauma, psychosomatic complaints or a sense of disconnection from the body. People with severe trauma or who find touch distressing should discuss this beforehand; some methods may be too intense.
cautions: Touch in therapy needs clear consent and boundaries. Body psychotherapist is not a protected title in the UK; check registration with an accredited body.
uk: Mainly private; some practitioners are registered with UKCP. Rarely offered on the NHS.
checkNotes: NICE CG178 grouping of body psychotherapy within 'arts therapies' is from secondary sources describing the guideline; I am fairly but not fully certain it is in the current published wording.

name: Authentic Movement
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with somatic and body-based approaches because it grew out of dance movement therapy, which the source puts in this family.
what: A practice in which a mover, usually with eyes closed, follows their own impulses to move while a witness watches attentively without judgement. Afterwards they talk about the experience. It aims to deepen self-awareness and the sense of being seen.
origin: Developed by dancer and teacher Mary Starks Whitehouse in the United States in the 1950s, influenced by Jungian ideas, and later developed by Janet Adler and others.
evidence: There is almost no controlled research. Its use rests on practitioner accounts and qualitative studies, so there is no evidence that it treats specific mental-health conditions.
practice: Usually small groups or pairs, in sessions from an hour to whole-day workshops or retreats. Movers move for a set time while one or more witnesses watch, then each speaks about what they noticed. It may be used within dance movement psychotherapy or as a personal practice.
suitability: Used by dancers, therapists and adults interested in body awareness and personal growth. It is not a standalone treatment for mental illness, and moving with eyes closed in a group may not suit people with trauma, dissociation or mobility difficulties.
cautions: Often led by facilitators who are not therapists. Not regulated in the UK.
uk: Workshops and groups run privately, sometimes by dance movement psychotherapists registered with ADMP UK. Not available on the NHS.
checkNotes: Family assigned by me (so); could arguably be cr.

name: Art Therapy
what: A form of psychotherapy that uses making art, such as drawing, painting or clay, as a main way of communicating. The images and the process of making them, together with the relationship with the therapist, help people express and work through feelings that may be hard to put into words. No artistic skill is needed.
origin: Developed in the 1940s: the term was coined in Britain by artist Adrian Hill in 1942, and Margaret Naumburg developed a psychoanalytic approach in the United States. The British Association of Art Therapists formed in 1964.
evidence: Trials and reviews give mixed results: some show benefits for symptoms and quality of life in various groups, but many studies are small. A large UK trial found group art therapy did not improve outcomes in schizophrenia. NICE guidance on psychosis and schizophrenia in adults says arts therapies can be considered, particularly for negative symptoms.
practice: Individual or group sessions, typically about an hour, weekly, from a few months to longer. You make art with materials provided and may talk about it with the therapist. Offered in NHS mental-health services, schools, hospices, prisons and private practice by HCPC-registered art therapists.
suitability: Used with children and adults with psychosis, trauma, depression, learning disabilities, autism, dementia and life-limiting illness, and with people who struggle to talk. It may suit less well those who want a highly structured, skills-based therapy.
cautions: Art therapist and art psychotherapist are protected titles; practitioners must be registered with the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). Check the HCPC register.
uk: NHS mental-health, child and adolescent and learning-disability services, schools, charities and private practice. Check the HCPC register; the British Association of Art Therapists has a directory.
checkNotes: NICE CG178 recommendation wording ('consider offering arts therapies... particularly for negative symptoms') confirmed via secondary sources; MATISSE trial result from memory.

name: Music Therapy
what: A psychological therapy in which a trained therapist uses live music-making, such as improvising on instruments or singing, and sometimes listening, to build a relationship and support communication, emotional expression and wellbeing. No musical ability is needed.
origin: Developed as a profession in the 1940s and 1950s, in the United States after work with war veterans and in Britain through pioneers such as Juliette Alvin, who founded a society for music therapy in 1958.
evidence: Reviews suggest benefits for depression, for some symptoms in schizophrenia, and for wellbeing and agitation in dementia, though many trials are small. Results in autism are mixed, with a large trial finding no effect on social symptoms. NICE psychosis guidance includes it among arts therapies that can be considered.
practice: Individual or group sessions, usually 30 to 60 minutes, weekly. You might play simple instruments, sing or improvise with the therapist, who responds musically. Delivered in hospitals, care homes, schools, hospices and private practice by HCPC-registered music therapists.
suitability: Used with children and adults with autism, learning disabilities, dementia, brain injury, psychosis, depression and in palliative care, especially when speech is limited. It may not suit people who are distressed by sound or music.
cautions: Music therapist is a protected title; practitioners must be registered with the HCPC. Music activities run by non-therapists are different from music therapy.
uk: NHS services, schools, charities, care homes and private practice. Check the HCPC register; the British Association for Music Therapy has a directory.
checkNotes: Juliette Alvin society founding year (1958) from memory.

name: Drama Therapy
what: A psychotherapy that uses drama and theatre techniques, such as role play, storytelling, improvisation, masks and puppets, to help people explore problems and try out new ways of seeing and responding. Distance created by stories and roles can make difficult feelings easier to approach.
origin: Developed in Britain from the 1960s and 1970s by pioneers including Peter Slade, who used the term in 1939, and Sue Jennings; the British Association of Dramatherapists formed in 1977. Related to Moreno's psychodrama.
evidence: Research consists mainly of small trials, qualitative and case studies, with some promising findings in psychosis, trauma and young people, but overall evidence is limited and low in quality. NICE psychosis guidance includes it among arts therapies that can be considered.
practice: Individual or group sessions, often about an hour, weekly. Activities might include warm-up games, acting out stories or scenes, using objects or puppets, and stepping out of role to reflect. Delivered in NHS, schools, prisons and private practice by HCPC-registered dramatherapists. No acting skill is needed.
suitability: Used with children and adults with emotional and behavioural difficulties, psychosis, learning disabilities, autism, trauma and in forensic settings. It may not suit people who find performing or role play very uncomfortable.
cautions: Drama therapist and dramatherapist are protected titles; practitioners must be registered with the HCPC.
uk: NHS, schools, charities, prisons and private practice. Check the HCPC register; the British Association of Dramatherapists has a directory.
checkNotes: Slade 1939 and BADth 1977 dates from memory; year set at approximate start of the UK profession (1960s).

name: Poetry Therapy
aka: Poetry and journal therapy; therapeutic writing
what: The use of reading and writing poetry and other forms of creative or reflective writing to support self-expression, understanding and emotional wellbeing. A facilitator chooses poems to discuss and invites people to write in response.
origin: Developed in the United States from the 1950s and 1960s by Eli Greifer, Jack Leedy and others; the National Association for Poetry Therapy was founded in 1981.
evidence: Evidence is limited to small studies and qualitative reports. Related research on expressive writing about emotional experiences shows small benefits in some groups, but there is little good-quality trial evidence for poetry therapy for specific mental-health conditions.
practice: Usually groups, sometimes individual, in sessions of about 60 to 90 minutes. A facilitator reads a poem aloud, the group discusses it, and participants write their own responses, which they may share. Offered in community, healthcare, education and private settings.
suitability: Used for wellbeing, grief, stress and recovery, and with people who enjoy words. It is not a substitute for treatment of severe mental illness, and may not suit people with literacy difficulties unless adapted.
cautions: Poetry therapist is not a protected or regulated title in the UK, and facilitators may not be trained clinicians.
uk: Mainly community groups, charities and private practitioners; the Lapidus organisation supports writing for wellbeing. Not a standard NHS therapy.
checkNotes: Founders and dates (Greifer, Leedy; NAPT 1981) from memory, not web-verified. Lapidus reference from memory.

name: Sandplay
what: A therapy in which a person creates scenes in a tray of sand using small figures and objects, while the therapist observes in a safe, accepting setting. The scenes are seen as expressing inner experiences that may be hard to put into words.
origin: Developed by Swiss Jungian analyst Dora Kalff in the 1950s and 1960s, building on Margaret Lowenfeld's World Technique, created in London in 1929.
evidence: Research is limited: mostly case studies and small trials, often with children, with some positive but low-quality findings. Its Jungian interpretations are not scientifically tested, and it is not recommended in NICE guidance.
practice: Usually individual sessions of about an hour, weekly, with children or adults. You choose figures from shelves and arrange them in a sand tray, sometimes adding water; the therapist may talk about it with you or simply witness. Often used by play therapists, art therapists and Jungian therapists.
suitability: Used especially with children, and adults who find talking difficult, for emotional and behavioural problems, trauma or grief. It may not suit people who want a structured, skills-based approach.
cautions: Sandplay therapist is not a regulated title. Check the practitioner's core professional registration.
uk: Offered by some play therapists, child psychotherapists, arts therapists and private practitioners; occasionally in schools and CAMHS.
checkNotes: Year 1956 approximate for Kalff's development of sandplay.

name: Play Therapy
aka: Child-centred play therapy; non-directive play therapy
what: A therapy for children that uses play, the natural way children communicate, to help them express feelings, make sense of experiences and develop coping. The therapist provides toys, art and other materials and a consistent, accepting relationship.
origin: Grew from the work of Anna Freud and Melanie Klein in the 1920s and 1930s; Virginia Axline described child-centred play therapy in the United States in 1947.
evidence: Meta-analyses report moderate benefits for children's emotional and behavioural problems, with stronger results when parents are involved, but many studies are small or of limited quality. It is not a main recommended treatment in NICE guidance for specific conditions.
practice: Usually individual weekly sessions of 40 to 50 minutes, for around 12 sessions to a year or more, in a playroom at a school, clinic or practice. The child chooses what to play with; the therapist follows, reflects and keeps the space safe. Parents usually have review meetings.
suitability: Used with children aged roughly 3 to 12 with emotional and behavioural difficulties, trauma, bereavement, anxiety or family change. Children with specific disorders may also need treatments with stronger evidence, such as parent training or CBT.
cautions: Play therapist is not a protected title, but the British Association of Play Therapists and Play Therapy UK run registers accredited by the Professional Standards Authority.
uk: Schools, charities, some CAMHS and private practice. Check the BAPT or PTUK registers.

name: Bibliotherapy
what: The use of reading to support mental health. It has two main forms: self-help books, often based on CBT, worked through alone or with support; and creative bibliotherapy, using fiction and poetry to prompt reflection and connection.
origin: The term was coined in the United States by Samuel Crothers in 1916; structured self-help bibliotherapy developed from the 1970s and 1980s.
evidence: Self-help books based on CBT have good evidence for mild to moderate depression and anxiety, especially with some guidance. NICE recommends guided self-help, which can use books, for less severe depression and for some anxiety disorders. Evidence for creative reading groups is limited.
practice: Self-help bibliotherapy involves reading and exercises over several weeks, sometimes with brief check-ins with a practitioner. Creative bibliotherapy is usually a reading group or one-to-one sessions discussing a text. Delivered via NHS Talking Therapies, libraries and community groups.
suitability: Self-help books suit people with mild to moderate anxiety or depression who are comfortable reading and working independently. They are less suitable for severe illness, crisis, or people with reading difficulties.
cautions: Book quality varies; evidence applies mainly to structured CBT-based books. Not a substitute for help in a crisis.
uk: NHS Talking Therapies guided self-help; the Reading Well scheme lets people borrow recommended books free from public libraries in England.
checkNotes: evidenceLevel 'strong' applies to CBT-based guided self-help bibliotherapy only; creative bibliotherapy has limited evidence.

name: PhotoTherapy
what: The use of personal photographs, family albums and photos people take or collect as prompts in counselling. Talking about images can bring up memories, feelings and ways of seeing oneself and others that are harder to reach through words alone.
origin: Developed by several therapists in North America in the 1970s; psychologist and art therapist Judy Weiser in Vancouver did much to define PhotoTherapy techniques.
evidence: Evidence is limited to case studies, qualitative research and small pilot studies. There are no good-quality trials showing it treats specific mental-health conditions.
practice: Individual or group sessions within counselling or arts therapy. You might bring family photos, take pictures on a theme, or arrange self-portraits, then talk about them with the therapist. Used by counsellors, art therapists and community practitioners.
suitability: Used for self-exploration, grief, identity and family issues, and with people who find visual prompts easier than talking. Old photos can unexpectedly bring up painful memories, so it may need care with people who have experienced trauma.
cautions: Not the same as light therapy for seasonal depression or skin conditions. Not a regulated title in the UK.
uk: Offered by some private counsellors, art therapists and community projects; not a standard NHS therapy.
checkNotes: Name read as photo-based counselling (Weiser), not light therapy. Founding year approximate (mid-1970s); not web-verified.

name: TM-based
what: A form of mantra meditation practised for about 20 minutes twice a day, sitting with eyes closed and silently repeating a sound. It is taught as an effortless technique for deep rest and reduced stress, and some programmes use it alongside mental-health care.
origin: Introduced by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi in India in 1955 and spread internationally from 1958 onwards, drawing on Hindu Vedic tradition.
evidence: Trials suggest modest benefits for anxiety, stress and blood pressure, and one trial in veterans with PTSD found it comparable with prolonged exposure, but many studies are small or linked to the TM organisation. It is not specifically recommended in NICE guidance for mental-health conditions.
practice: Taught by certified teachers in a standard course of about four sessions, starting with one-to-one instruction, then group follow-ups. You then practise alone for about 20 minutes twice daily. Courses usually charge a fee.
suitability: Used by adults for stress, anxiety and general wellbeing. It is not a substitute for treatment of severe mental illness; people with psychosis or severe trauma should discuss meditation with their clinician.
cautions: Teaching is controlled by the TM organisation and course fees can be substantial. Meditation can occasionally bring up distressing experiences.
uk: Through the TM organisation's UK centres and teachers; not available on the NHS.
checkNotes: PTSD trial (Nidich et al. 2018, veterans, non-inferior to prolonged exposure) and 'TM international from 1958' from memory. evidenceLevel 'moderate' is a judgement given conflict-of-interest concerns; could be 'limited'.

name: MSC
what: A structured group programme that teaches mindfulness and self-compassion skills: responding to one's own suffering, mistakes and difficulties with the kindness one might offer a friend. It aims to reduce harsh self-criticism and increase resilience.
origin: Developed by psychologists Kristin Neff and Christopher Germer in the United States around 2010; the first randomised trial was published in 2013.
evidence: Randomised trials, mostly in non-clinical groups, show improvements in self-compassion, wellbeing, stress, anxiety and depressive symptoms. Evidence for diagnosed mental-health conditions is still emerging, and it is not in NICE guidance.
practice: Usually eight weekly group sessions of about 2.5 to 3 hours, plus a half-day retreat, in person or online. Includes guided meditations, exercises, discussion and home practice. Led by trained MSC teachers.
suitability: Used by adults with stress, self-criticism or burnout, and by health professionals. Turning towards difficult emotions can initially increase distress ('backdraft'), so it may not suit people in acute crisis or with severe trauma without additional support.
cautions: MSC teachers are not regulated in the UK; check teacher training. Courses are educational rather than therapy.
uk: Mainly private courses and online programmes run by trained teachers; occasionally offered within NHS staff wellbeing schemes.

name: Mindfulness-Based Stress
what: An eight-week group course that teaches mindfulness meditation and gentle yoga as ways to relate differently to stress, pain and difficult thoughts, by paying attention to the present moment without judgement. Its offshoot, MBCT, adds elements of cognitive therapy to prevent relapse into depression.
origin: Developed by Jon Kabat-Zinn at the University of Massachusetts Medical School in 1979, drawing on Buddhist meditation in a secular form. MBCT was developed by Segal, Williams and Teasdale around 2000.
evidence: Many trials and meta-analyses show moderate benefits for stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms and coping with chronic illness. MBCT has strong evidence for preventing relapse in recurrent depression and is recommended by NICE for this; NICE also includes group mindfulness and meditation as an option for less severe depression.
practice: Groups of about 10 to 30 people meet weekly for eight sessions of around 2 to 2.5 hours, plus a day of practice. Includes body scan, sitting meditation, mindful movement, discussion and around 45 minutes of daily home practice. Led by trained mindfulness teachers.
suitability: Used for stress, chronic pain, long-term health conditions and mild to moderate anxiety and depression; MBCT for people with recurrent depression who are currently well. It may not suit people in acute crisis, with active psychosis or with severe unprocessed trauma.
cautions: Meditation can occasionally increase anxiety or bring up traumatic memories. Teachers are not statutorily regulated; UK good-practice guidelines list trained teachers.
uk: MBCT through some NHS Talking Therapies services; MBSR mainly private, workplace or university courses. The British Association of Mindfulness-Based Approaches lists teachers.
checkNotes: evidenceLevel 'strong' rests mainly on MBCT's NICE recommendation (NG222) for relapse prevention; MBSR itself is closer to moderate. Editor: evidence label set to moderate for MBSR itself; NICE’s recommendation is for its relative MBCT.

name: Vipassana-based
aka: Insight meditation; Vipassana (as taught by S. N. Goenka and others)
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed in mindfulness and meditation because it is a meditation practice and an important root of modern mindfulness programmes.
what: Insight meditation from the Theravada Buddhist tradition, which trains close, non-reactive attention to breath and bodily sensations to see how experience arises and passes. Modern versions are taught in secular or semi-secular courses, and some programmes use it in prisons or for addiction.
origin: An ancient Buddhist practice; modern lay teaching spread from Burma in the 20th century, and S. N. Goenka popularised 10-day residential courses internationally from 1969.
evidence: There is limited direct evidence: small and non-randomised studies, for example in prisons and with substance use, report reduced substance use and improved wellbeing. Most strong mindfulness evidence comes from programmes like MBSR and MBCT rather than traditional Vipassana retreats.
practice: Commonly a 10-day silent residential retreat with around ten hours of meditation a day, no talking, phones or reading, and evening talks; Goenka courses are free, funded by donations. Shorter courses and weekly groups also exist. Taught by meditation teachers, not therapists.
suitability: Used by adults interested in meditation for wellbeing or spiritual practice. Intensive silent retreats may not suit people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe depression or trauma, and organisers often screen for this.
cautions: Intensive retreats have been linked to rare reports of severe anxiety, depersonalisation or psychotic episodes. It is not a treatment for mental illness and is not regulated.
uk: Residential centres and local groups run by meditation organisations; not available on the NHS.
checkNotes: Goenka start date (1969) and prison/substance-use study findings from memory, not web-verified. Year null because the practice is traditional.

name: Zen Therapy
aka: Zen Therapy (David Brazier); Zen-informed psychotherapy; related to Morita therapy
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed in mindfulness and meditation because it applies Zen Buddhist meditation and ideas to therapy.
what: An approach that brings Zen Buddhist ideas and practices, such as sitting meditation, acceptance of experience as it is, and attention to everyday action, into counselling. Rather than fixing problems directly, it aims to help people loosen their grip on rigid ideas of self and live more fully in the present.
origin: Zen has long influenced Western therapy; British psychotherapist David Brazier set out a Zen Therapy approach in a 1995 book. Earlier, Japanese psychiatrist Shoma Morita developed Zen-influenced Morita therapy around 1919.
evidence: There is little formal research on Zen Therapy as such. Related Morita therapy has some small trials, mainly in Asia, and broader mindfulness approaches have stronger evidence, but these findings cannot be assumed to apply.
practice: Usually individual counselling sessions, sometimes combined with meditation groups or retreats. Sessions may involve talking, sitting quietly, and exploring how attachment to beliefs and desires shapes distress. Offered by therapists with a Buddhist training background.
suitability: Used by adults interested in Buddhist ideas, seeking help with anxiety, life transitions or meaning. It is not an established treatment for specific mental-health conditions and may not suit people wanting a structured, symptom-focused therapy.
cautions: Not a protected title in the UK. Check the practitioner's core training and accredited registration.
uk: A small number of private practitioners and Buddhist-influenced training organisations; not available on the NHS. Some practitioners are BACP or UKCP registered.
checkNotes: Name is ambiguous: read as Zen-informed psychotherapy, especially David Brazier's Zen Therapy (1995 book); it could instead refer to Morita therapy or general Zen-influenced practice. Brazier and Morita dates from memory.

name: Equine Therapy
aka: Equine-assisted psychotherapy (EAP); equine-facilitated psychotherapy; equine-assisted learning
what: Therapy in which a mental health professional works alongside horses, usually on the ground rather than riding. Clients groom, lead or observe horses, and the horse's reactions are used as live feedback on the client's behaviour, emotions and relationships, giving material to reflect on with the therapist.
origin: Grew from therapeutic riding in Europe and North America; ground-based equine psychotherapy was formalised in the US in the 1990s, with organisations such as EAGALA (founded 1999) training practitioners.
evidence: Studies are mostly small, uncontrolled or poorly controlled, with some reports of reduced trauma, anxiety or behaviour symptoms in children, adolescents and veterans. Systematic reviews describe the evidence as promising but low quality, and it is hard to separate effects of the horse from attention, being outdoors and the therapeutic relationship.
practice: Individual, family or group sessions at a stables or farm, often 60 to 90 minutes, weekly for several weeks. A therapist and an equine specialist work together. Activities include grooming, leading horses through tasks and reflecting on what happened.
suitability: Offered to children and young people with emotional or behavioural difficulties, people with trauma histories, and those who find talking therapy hard. Not suitable for people with severe allergies, fear of horses, or some physical limitations.
cautions: Horses are large animals and injuries can occur, so supervision and insurance matter. Training and titles in this field are not regulated in the UK; check the practitioner's core mental health qualification and professional registration.
uk: Mostly private or charity-run, sometimes commissioned by schools, local authorities or charities. Look for a therapist registered with BACP, UKCP or HCPC working alongside a qualified equine specialist.

name: Canine-Assisted
aka: Dog-assisted therapy; animal-assisted therapy (AAT) with dogs; pet therapy
what: A trained dog takes part in sessions led by a health or mental health professional. The dog's presence is meant to lower stress, help people feel safe and build rapport, and can be used in planned therapeutic activities. It differs from casual therapy-dog visits, which aim at comfort rather than specific treatment goals.
origin: US child psychologist Boris Levinson described his dog Jingles as a 'co-therapist' in the early 1960s; animal-assisted therapy developed from the 1970s onwards in the US and UK.
evidence: Small trials and reviews suggest short-term reductions in anxiety, stress and agitation in settings such as hospitals, care homes and schools, with some positive results for children with autism and adults with depression. Studies are generally small, short and hard to blind, so evidence for lasting clinical benefit is limited.
practice: The dog and its handler join individual or group sessions in clinics, hospitals, schools, care homes or prisons. Sessions are usually 30 to 60 minutes. Activities range from stroking and walking the dog to structured tasks linked to therapy goals.
suitability: Used with children, older people, people with dementia, autistic people and people in hospital or secure settings. Not suitable for people with dog allergies, phobias, or where infection control is a concern.
cautions: Animal welfare, hygiene, infection control and bites need to be managed. Dogs should be temperament-assessed. There is no statutory regulation of animal-assisted therapy in the UK.
uk: Mainly through charities (for example Pets As Therapy visits) and some NHS, school or private services; animal-assisted therapy sessions are mostly private.

name: Dolphin Therapy
what: Programmes in which a person, often a child with a disability, swims or interacts with captive dolphins, sometimes combined with other therapy. Promoters claim that dolphin contact or dolphin sonar improves attention, learning, mood or development; these claims are not supported by credible evidence.
origin: Popularised by US psychologist David Nathanson in Florida from the late 1970s; commercial programmes later spread to Mexico, the Caribbean, Ukraine and elsewhere.
evidence: Published studies have serious design flaws, and independent reviews conclude there is no good evidence of specific or lasting benefit. Any short-term mood improvement is likely explained by novelty, excitement and attention rather than anything particular to dolphins. Claims about healing sonar have no scientific basis.
practice: Usually a costly package, often abroad, of short daily sessions over one to two weeks at a marine park or facility. Children swim, touch or play with dolphins under trainers' supervision, sometimes alongside physiotherapy or speech therapy.
suitability: Marketed mainly to families of children with autism, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome and other disabilities. It is not recommended in NHS or professional guidance.
cautions: Dolphins can bite or injure people and can transmit infections. Animal-welfare groups strongly oppose capturing and confining dolphins for these programmes. Costs and travel can be high for families with no expected specific benefit.
uk: Not available in the UK, which has no captive dolphins. Not provided by the NHS; families who pursue it travel abroad privately.

name: Animal-Assisted Play
what: Combines play therapy with an animal, usually a dog, as part of the session. Children play and interact with the animal and therapist, and the relationship with the animal is used to help children express feelings, practise empathy and self-control, and build trust. The animal's wellbeing and consent are treated as part of the work.
origin: Developed by US psychologist Risë VanFleet and UK animal-assisted therapist Tracie Faa-Thompson in the 2000s, building on child-centred play therapy and filial therapy.
evidence: Evidence is mainly case studies, practitioner reports and small studies. There are no substantial controlled trials showing that adding an animal improves outcomes over play therapy alone.
practice: Individual or family sessions, often weekly for around 45 to 60 minutes, in a playroom or outdoors. A trained play therapist works with their own animal, using games, training tasks and free play.
suitability: Used with children who have experienced trauma, attachment difficulties, anxiety or behavioural problems, and with families. Not suitable where a child is fearful of or rough with animals, or has allergies.
cautions: Requires attention to bite risk, hygiene and the animal's stress. No statutory regulation of play therapists or animal-assisted practitioners in the UK.
uk: Private practitioners and some charities. Check registration with a body such as BAPT, Play Therapy UK, BACP or UKCP and specific animal-assisted training.
checkNotes: Year 2008 is an approximation (VanFleet's book Play Therapy with Kids and Canines appeared in 2008; the AAPT model was formalised around then and in a later 2017 book). Could not confirm an exact founding date.

name: Therapeutic Riding
aka: Riding for disabled people; adaptive riding; related to hippotherapy (horse-based physiotherapy)
what: Horse riding adapted for disabled people, aimed at physical, emotional and social benefits such as balance, posture, confidence and enjoyment. It is usually taught by riding instructors rather than therapists, unlike hippotherapy, where a physiotherapist or occupational therapist uses the horse's movement as treatment.
origin: Developed in Scandinavia and Britain in the 1950s, inspired partly by Danish rider Lis Hartel, who won an Olympic medal in 1952 after polio. The UK Riding for the Disabled Association was founded in 1969.
evidence: Reviews find some evidence that hippotherapy and riding improve balance and gross motor function in children with cerebral palsy. A few trials in autistic children report reductions in irritability and hyperactivity. Studies are generally small and of mixed quality, and evidence for mental health outcomes is limited.
practice: Group or individual riding sessions of about 30 to 60 minutes, often weekly, at a riding centre. Volunteers lead the horse and walk alongside. Activities include riding exercises, games and horse care.
suitability: Used for children and adults with physical, learning or sensory disabilities, including cerebral palsy, autism and multiple sclerosis. Not suitable for some conditions affecting the spine or joints, or for heavier riders above a centre's limits.
cautions: Falls are the main risk; helmets and suitably trained staff and horses are essential. Medical clearance may be needed for some conditions.
uk: Widely available through Riding for the Disabled Association (RDA) groups, mostly charity-funded. Hippotherapy is offered by some private physiotherapists.
checkNotes: Year 1952 marks Lis Hartel's influence rather than a formal founding; approximate.

name: Wilderness Therapy
what: Extended stays in remote outdoor settings, often backcountry expeditions lasting weeks, combined with group and individual therapy. The idea is that living simply, facing natural challenges and depending on a group builds responsibility, coping skills and self-esteem. It is most common in the United States for adolescents.
origin: Grew from Outward Bound (founded 1941) and US university and outdoor programmes of the 1960s and 1970s; a commercial industry for troubled teenagers expanded in the US from the 1980s.
evidence: Outcome studies, mostly uncontrolled, report improvements in behaviour and wellbeing, but rigorous controlled trials are scarce and many studies are run by the industry. Serious harms are documented in some US programmes, including deaths from exposure, dehydration, restraint and neglect, described in a 2007 US GAO investigation and later reports.
practice: Small groups hike and camp for several weeks to months, learning outdoor skills, with therapy sessions in the field from licensed clinicians and support from field staff. In the US, young people are sometimes enrolled by parents against their will, and sometimes transported by escort services.
suitability: Offered for adolescents and young adults with behavioural problems, substance use or family conflict. Not suitable for people with medical conditions that make remote living unsafe, or where coercion would be harmful.
cautions: Investigations in the US have documented abuse, neglect and deaths in some programmes, with weak oversight. Involuntary placement and transport raise serious ethical concerns. Ask about clinical oversight, medical cover, accreditation and complaints procedures.
uk: Not an NHS treatment. Some UK charities and private providers run outdoor therapeutic programmes, usually shorter and voluntary; there is no specific regulation of wilderness therapy.
checkNotes: Year 1970 is an approximation for the emergence of US wilderness therapy programmes. Chose evidenceLevel 'limited' rather than 'harmful' because harms are documented in specific programmes rather than in the approach as a whole; editors may wish to review.

name: Adventure Therapy
what: Uses planned, challenging activities such as climbing, canoeing, ropes courses and group problem-solving tasks, usually outdoors, as the basis for therapy. Facing manageable risk and working as a group are meant to build confidence, trust and coping, with reflection afterwards linking the experience to everyday life.
origin: Rooted in Kurt Hahn's Outward Bound, founded in Aberdyfi, Wales, in 1941, and the US Project Adventure (1971), with therapeutic adaptations developing from the 1970s and 1980s.
evidence: Meta-analyses report small to moderate short-term improvements in self-esteem, behaviour and wellbeing, mainly in young people. Most studies lack strong controls or long-term follow-up, so evidence for specific mental health conditions is limited.
practice: Group-based, from single days to residential courses of several days, led by outdoor instructors with a therapist or counsellor. Activities are followed by group discussion to draw out learning.
suitability: Used with young people in schools, youth services and mental health services, and with adults in substance use recovery or veterans' programmes. May not suit people with physical limitations or very high anxiety without adaptation.
cautions: Physical risks need qualified instructors and risk assessment. Challenge should be voluntary; pressure to participate can be counterproductive.
uk: Through charities, outdoor education centres, some CAMHS and youth services, and private providers. Not regulated as a therapy; check instructor and therapist qualifications.
checkNotes: Year chosen as 1971 (Project Adventure); Outward Bound dates from 1941 but was educational rather than therapeutic.

name: Ecotherapy
aka: Nature-based therapy; green care; green social prescribing; outdoor therapy
what: An umbrella term for therapeutic activities in nature, such as conservation work, therapeutic gardening, care farming and walking or talking therapy outdoors. It draws on the idea that contact with nature reduces stress and improves mood, and that meaningful outdoor activity with others supports recovery.
origin: The term was popularised by US pastoral counsellor Howard Clinebell's 1996 book, alongside 1990s ecopsychology; in the UK, the charity Mind promoted ecotherapy from 2007.
evidence: Many studies link time in green space with lower stress and better mood, and evaluations of UK nature-based programmes report improved wellbeing. Controlled trials for clinical conditions are few and often small, so benefit beyond general wellbeing is not well established.
practice: Usually group-based, weekly sessions of a few hours over several weeks, in gardens, parks, woodlands or farms. Led by charities, horticultural therapists or counsellors. Activities include gardening, conservation tasks, walks and reflection.
suitability: Used for people with mild to moderate depression, anxiety and stress, social isolation, and people recovering from mental illness. May not suit people with limited mobility unless sites are accessible.
cautions: Weather, terrain and allergies need consideration. 'Ecotherapist' is not a protected title in the UK.
uk: Through social prescribing link workers in GP surgeries, NHS green social prescribing schemes, Mind and other charities, and private outdoor therapists.

name: Forest Bathing
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with animal and nature therapies because it is a nature-based practice.
what: Spending slow, unhurried time in a forest, paying attention to sights, sounds, smells and textures rather than exercising or hiking to a goal. The aim is relaxation and stress reduction through sensory contact with the natural environment.
origin: The term shinrin-yoku was coined in Japan in 1982 by Tomohide Akiyama of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries as part of a public health and forestry initiative.
evidence: Many studies, largely from Japan, Korea and China, report short-term reductions in stress, anxiety and low mood and changes in measures such as heart rate and cortisol. Most are small and short, with limited blinding and follow-up, so effects on clinical conditions are uncertain.
practice: Guided walks of about two to three hours, in groups or alone, at a gentle pace with invitations to notice the surroundings, sit quietly and reflect. Guides are often certified by private training organisations.
suitability: Used for general stress and wellbeing. Not a treatment for serious mental illness. May not suit people with limited mobility, severe allergies or anxiety about being outdoors.
cautions: Ticks, weather and uneven ground are practical risks. Guide certifications are not regulated.
uk: Private guides, some woodland trusts, and occasionally social prescribing schemes. Not an NHS treatment.

name: Solution-Focused
what: A short, goal-directed talking therapy that focuses on what the person wants to be different and what is already working, rather than on the causes of problems. Techniques include the 'miracle question' and scaling questions, used to identify strengths, small steps and signs of progress.
origin: Developed by Steve de Shazer, Insoo Kim Berg and colleagues at the Brief Family Therapy Center in Milwaukee, USA, from the late 1970s and early 1980s.
evidence: Meta-analyses of controlled studies show small to moderate benefits across problems including depression, behaviour problems in children and wellbeing, broadly similar to other therapies. Many studies are small or of modest quality. It is not specifically recommended for particular conditions in NICE guidance.
practice: Usually individual, sometimes couple, family or group, typically three to eight sessions of about 50 minutes. Delivered by counsellors, psychologists, social workers and others in schools, health and social care. Conversations centre on goals, exceptions and next steps.
suitability: Used for a wide range of everyday difficulties, in schools, youth work, primary care and organisations. May be less suited on its own to severe or complex mental illness, or to people who want to explore their past in depth.
uk: Offered in some NHS, school and social care services and by private practitioners. Check registration with BACP, UKCP or another accredited register; the UK Association for Solution Focused Practice supports practitioners.

name: Brief Strategic
aka: MRI brief therapy; Palo Alto model; also used for Nardone's brief strategic therapy (distinct from Brief Strategic Family Therapy, BSFT)
what: A short, problem-focused therapy based on the idea that problems are kept going by the very solutions people keep trying. The therapist identifies these 'attempted solutions' and helps the person or family try something different, sometimes using reframing, paradoxical tasks or experiments between sessions.
origin: Developed at the Mental Research Institute's Brief Therapy Center in Palo Alto, California, founded in 1966 by Richard Fisch, John Weakland and Paul Watzlawick; extended in Italy by Giorgio Nardone from the late 1980s.
evidence: Evidence for the MRI and Nardone models comes mostly from case series and uncontrolled outcome studies, with few randomised trials. The separate Brief Strategic Family Therapy model for adolescent drug use and behaviour problems has several US trials with mixed results.
practice: Individual, couple or family sessions, usually up to about ten. The therapist asks detailed questions about how the problem happens and what has been tried, then sets specific tasks to carry out between sessions.
suitability: Used for anxiety, phobias, obsessive problems, family and relationship conflict and behavioural problems. Some people may find directive or paradoxical tasks uncomfortable.
uk: Mainly from private practitioners and some family therapists. Check registration with UKCP, BACP or AFT (Association for Family Therapy).
checkNotes: Name is ambiguous: interpreted as the MRI/Nardone brief strategic therapy; could alternatively mean Szapocznik's Brief Strategic Family Therapy (BSFT, Miami, 1970s), which has a stronger trial base.

name: Single Session
aka: Single-session therapy (SST); single-session interventions; one-at-a-time therapy
what: An approach that treats each session as potentially complete in itself, aiming to help the person make useful progress in one meeting, with more sessions available if needed. It is based on the observation that many people attend only once and that a single focused session can make a difference.
origin: Described by Moshe Talmon, Michael Hoyt and Robert Rosenbaum at Kaiser Permanente in California in the late 1980s; Talmon's book Single-Session Therapy appeared in 1990.
evidence: Meta-analyses of randomised trials, particularly of brief structured single-session interventions for young people, show small but meaningful improvements in anxiety, depression and behaviour problems. Effects are modest and research on longer-term outcomes is still developing.
practice: One planned session, often 60 to 90 minutes, sometimes walk-in or online, focused on the person's most pressing concern, with a plan for afterwards. Some versions are short self-guided online programmes.
suitability: Used in walk-in clinics, CAMHS, student services and charities to reduce waiting times and support people with mild to moderate difficulties. Not a replacement for ongoing care for severe or complex problems or high risk.
cautions: Services should have clear routes to further help and risk assessment.
uk: Offered by some NHS CAMHS and adult services, charities and youth services, and private therapists; check registration with BACP, UKCP or HCPC.

name: Clinical Hypnosis
what: The use of hypnosis, a state of focused attention and heightened responsiveness to suggestion, by a trained practitioner as part of treatment. It is usually combined with other approaches such as CBT, relaxation or pain management, rather than being a therapy on its own.
origin: Scottish surgeon James Braid coined the term 'hypnosis' in the early 1840s, building on earlier mesmerism; modern clinical and research hypnosis developed in the 20th century.
evidence: There is good evidence for gut-directed hypnotherapy for irritable bowel syndrome, and moderate evidence for pain and procedural anxiety. NICE guidance on IBS includes hypnotherapy as an option when medicines have not helped. Evidence for smoking cessation, depression and other mental health conditions is limited or mixed.
practice: Individual sessions of about 50 to 60 minutes, often four to twelve sessions, sometimes with recordings for home practice. The practitioner guides the person into a relaxed, focused state and uses suggestions and imagery linked to their goals.
suitability: Used for irritable bowel syndrome, pain, anxiety around medical procedures, and habit change. Use with caution in people with psychosis or dissociative conditions.
cautions: Hypnotherapists are not statutorily regulated in the UK. Hypnosis should not be used to 'recover' memories, because it can create false memories and increase confidence in them.
uk: Some NHS gastroenterology services offer gut-directed hypnotherapy. Otherwise private; health professionals may belong to BSCAH; other hypnotherapists may be on the CNHC or another accredited register.

name: Ericksonian
what: A style of hypnosis and therapy based on the work of Milton Erickson, using indirect suggestion, metaphor, stories and the person's own language and resources rather than formal commands. It treats the unconscious as a source of solutions and tailors each intervention to the individual.
origin: Developed by US psychiatrist Milton H. Erickson (1901–1980), mainly in Phoenix, Arizona, from the 1930s to the 1970s; he founded the American Society of Clinical Hypnosis in 1957.
evidence: Erickson's methods are documented largely through case reports and teaching. There are few controlled trials of Ericksonian therapy specifically, and studies comparing indirect with direct suggestion show no clear advantage. Evidence for benefit beyond hypnosis generally is limited.
practice: Individual sessions, often short-term, where the therapist talks conversationally, tells stories and uses metaphors, sometimes without a formal trance induction.
suitability: Used for anxiety, habits, pain and personal change. People who prefer explicit, structured methods may find it vague. Use with caution in psychosis or dissociative conditions.
cautions: Hypnotherapy is not statutorily regulated in the UK; check training and registration.
uk: Private practitioners; some are on the CNHC or other accredited registers, or are health professionals belonging to BSCAH.
checkNotes: Year 1957 (founding of ASCH) is a marker; Erickson's approach developed gradually from the 1930s.

name: Regression Therapy
aka: Hypnotic age regression; includes past-life regression
what: Uses hypnosis or guided imagery to take a person 'back' to earlier experiences, often childhood or, in past-life regression, supposed previous lives, on the belief that uncovering and re-experiencing these memories will resolve current problems.
origin: Age regression appears in hypnosis from the late 19th century; past-life regression was popularised in the US from the 1970s by Morris Netherton and later by Brian Weiss's 1988 book.
evidence: There is no credible evidence that regression therapy treats mental health conditions, and memory research shows that hypnosis and suggestive techniques can create vivid false memories. In the 1990s, recovered-memory practices led to false abuse allegations and family breakdown, prompting warnings from the British Psychological Society and Royal College of Psychiatrists.
practice: Individual sessions, often one to two hours, in which the practitioner induces relaxation or trance and invites the person to recall or imagine earlier events and talk about them.
suitability: Not recommended for any mental health condition. It is particularly unsuitable for people seeking to discover whether abuse happened, and for people with dissociation or psychosis.
cautions: Memories produced in regression are unreliable and can feel completely real. Professional bodies advise against using hypnosis to recover memories. Unregulated field in the UK.
uk: Private, unregulated practitioners only; not provided by the NHS.
checkNotes: Year 1970 is approximate (popularisation of past-life regression); age regression in hypnosis is older. evidenceLevel set to 'none' although documented harms from recovered-memory work could justify 'harmful'; editors may wish to review.

name: Parts Therapy
aka: Tebbetts/Hunter parts therapy; ego-part work in hypnosis (not the same as Internal Family Systems)
what: A hypnotherapy technique in which the person, in trance, is helped to identify and 'talk to' different parts of their personality that are in conflict, such as a part that wants to change and a part that resists. The therapist mediates between parts to reach an agreement. It is distinct from Internal Family Systems (IFS), a separate non-hypnotic psychotherapy.
origin: Pioneered by US hypnotherapist Charles Tebbetts from roughly the 1960s to 1980s and systematised by his student Roy Hunter, whose book on parts therapy was published in 2005.
evidence: Evidence consists of practitioner case reports and training literature. No controlled trials of this specific technique were found.
practice: Individual hypnotherapy sessions, often 60 to 90 minutes, sometimes one to a few sessions. After a trance induction, the practitioner invites parts to 'speak', asks about their intentions and negotiates a resolution.
suitability: Used by hypnotherapists for habits, inner conflict and self-sabotage. Not suitable for people with dissociative identity disorder, psychosis or severe trauma unless the practitioner is clinically trained.
cautions: Hypnotherapists are not statutorily regulated in the UK. As with other hypnotic work, suggestion can shape what emerges.
uk: Private hypnotherapists only; some are on the CNHC or other accredited registers.
checkNotes: Source named 'Roy Hunt'; this appears to be Roy Hunter, student of Charles Tebbetts. Year 1970 is an approximation; no primary source found for when Tebbetts first developed the technique.

name: Eclectic
what: A therapist draws techniques from several different therapies, choosing what seems most helpful for each person and problem, rather than following one model. Unlike integrative therapy, it does not necessarily combine theories into a single framework; the emphasis is on practical choice of methods.
origin: Advocated by US psychologist Frederick Thorne around 1950; Arnold Lazarus described 'technical eclecticism' in 1967 and later his multimodal therapy.
evidence: Because eclectic therapy differs from one therapist to the next, it has rarely been tested as such. Research shows that the therapeutic relationship and other common factors matter across therapies, but there is little evidence on whether eclectic choice of methods improves outcomes.
practice: Usually individual sessions of about 50 minutes, short- or long-term. The therapist might use CBT techniques, person-centred listening and other methods depending on the person's needs.
suitability: Common in private and voluntary-sector counselling for a wide range of everyday difficulties. People with specific conditions with recommended treatments may be better served by those.
cautions: Quality depends heavily on the therapist's training in each method used; ask what they are trained in.
uk: Widely offered by private counsellors and charities. Check registration with BACP, UKCP, NCPS or another PSA-accredited register.

name: Integrative
what: Brings together ideas and methods from different schools, such as psychodynamic, humanistic and cognitive-behavioural, into a coherent framework adapted to the individual. The relationship between therapist and client is usually seen as central.
origin: The psychotherapy integration movement grew in the 1970s and 1980s, marked by the founding of the Society for the Exploration of Psychotherapy Integration in 1983; there is no single founder.
evidence: Integrative therapy is a broad category, so it is hard to test as a whole. Some specific integrative models, such as cognitive analytic therapy and schema therapy, have trial evidence for particular conditions, and talking therapies in general show benefit, but generic integrative counselling has fewer rigorous trials.
practice: Usually individual weekly sessions of about 50 minutes, short- or long-term, in private practice, charities, GP surgeries or student services. The therapist adapts the approach as therapy progresses.
suitability: Used for a wide range of emotional and relationship difficulties. For some conditions, NICE recommends specific therapies instead.
uk: Widely available privately and through charities and some NHS services. Check registration with UKCP, BACP or another PSA-accredited register.
checkNotes: evidenceLevel 'moderate' reflects trial evidence for specific integrative models; generic integrative counselling might be rated 'limited'.

name: Narrative Therapy
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with systemic and family therapies because it emerged from family therapy and is often taught within that field.
what: Sees people's lives as shaped by the stories they tell about themselves. The therapist helps the person 'externalise' the problem, treating it as separate from who they are, and find overlooked experiences that support a preferred story. It pays attention to how culture and power shape these stories.
origin: Developed by Michael White in Adelaide, Australia, and David Epston in Auckland, New Zealand, in the 1980s; their key book appeared in 1990 as Narrative Means to Therapeutic Ends.
evidence: Research consists mainly of qualitative studies, case reports and small trials, with some positive findings for depression, family conflict and children's problems. There are few large or high-quality randomised trials, so evidence is limited.
practice: Individual, couple, family or group sessions, often weekly, with varying numbers. The therapist asks questions to explore the problem's effects and alternative stories, and may write letters or certificates, or invite 'outsider witnesses' to listen.
suitability: Used with children and families, communities and people dealing with trauma, grief or marginalisation. Some may prefer a more structured, skills-based approach.
uk: Offered by some family therapists in NHS CAMHS and by private practitioners. Check registration with AFT, UKCP or BACP.

name: Peer Support
aka: Peer support work; mutual aid; lived-experience support
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed in mixed/other because it is a form of support based on shared lived experience rather than a specific therapeutic model.
what: Support from people who have lived experience of similar mental health or other difficulties, either informally through mutual-aid groups or through trained, paid peer support workers in services. It aims to offer hope, understanding, practical help and connection based on shared experience rather than professional expertise.
origin: Has diverse roots, including mutual-aid groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous (1935) and the psychiatric survivor and user movements from the 1970s; formal peer support worker roles grew in the 2000s.
evidence: Reviews of randomised trials find peer support in mental health services produces similar clinical outcomes to standard care, with some evidence of improved hope, empowerment and sense of recovery, but little evidence of reduced symptoms. Study quality is often low.
practice: One-to-one or group, in person or online. Peer workers may meet people in hospital, the community or crisis services; mutual-aid groups meet regularly, often weekly. It involves sharing experiences, problem-solving and accompanying people to activities.
suitability: Used alongside other care for people with mental illness, addiction, long-term conditions and carers. It is not a replacement for clinical treatment when that is needed.
cautions: Peer workers need training, supervision and support; boundaries and confidentiality should be clear.
uk: Peer support workers are employed in many NHS mental health trusts; groups are run by charities such as Mind and by mutual-aid fellowships, usually free.
checkNotes: Year 1970 is an approximation for a practice with diverse origins. Did not state NICE status: NICE psychosis guidance (CG178) is believed to suggest considering peer support, but this was not verified.

name: VR Therapy
aka: Virtual reality exposure therapy (VRET); VR-assisted therapy
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed in digital and technology because it is delivered through VR headsets and software.
what: Uses virtual reality headsets to place people in computer-generated situations, such as heights, flying or busy streets, so they can practise facing feared situations safely and gradually. Most VR therapy is a form of exposure therapy or CBT, sometimes guided by an automated virtual coach.
origin: First tested by Barbara Rothbaum and Larry Hodges at Emory University and Georgia Tech, USA, in 1995 for fear of heights; later developed for other phobias, PTSD and psychosis.
evidence: Meta-analyses show VR exposure works about as well as real-life exposure for specific phobias and some anxiety disorders. A large UK trial of automated VR therapy (gameChange) reduced agoraphobic avoidance in people with psychosis, particularly those with severe avoidance. Evidence for PTSD and other conditions is more mixed.
practice: Individual sessions, often six to twelve of 30 to 60 minutes, in a clinic or at home, wearing a headset. A therapist or virtual coach guides the person through graded scenarios and coping techniques.
suitability: Used for phobias, social anxiety, PTSD and agoraphobic avoidance in psychosis. NICE has conditionally recommended gameChange for severe agoraphobic avoidance in psychosis while more evidence is gathered. May not suit people with severe motion sickness, epilepsy or some visual problems.
cautions: Headsets can cause motion sickness, eye strain or disorientation. Consumer VR apps marketed for mental health are often untested.
uk: Limited NHS availability in some mental health trusts and research services; some private clinics. Check the clinician's registration with HCPC, BABCP or BACP.
checkNotes: NICE early value assessment (HTE15/HTG701) of gameChange: recommends use with evidence generation for people aged 16 and over; exact current wording and status not fully verified.

name: AI-Assisted
aka: AI chatbots for mental health; conversational agents; AI tools used alongside human therapy
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed in digital and technology because it relies on software and artificial intelligence.
what: Covers chatbots that offer CBT-style conversations, general AI assistants people use for emotional support, and AI tools used by services for triage, note-taking or between-session support. The idea is to widen access and provide support at any time, though these tools are not equivalent to a qualified therapist.
origin: Early ancestor: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA program at MIT (1966). Rule-based CBT chatbots such as Woebot appeared from 2017; generative AI chatbots based on large language models spread from 2022.
evidence: Small trials of structured chatbots show short-term reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms; a 2025 trial of a generative AI chatbot reported benefits versus a waiting list, under clinician monitoring. Evidence is early, mostly short-term, often industry-funded, and there are documented cases of chatbots responding unsafely to people in crisis.
practice: Usually self-directed text conversations on a phone app or website, at any time, sometimes as part of a service with human oversight. In some services AI is used for referral, assessment questions or session notes rather than therapy.
suitability: May help some people with mild symptoms, as self-help, or while waiting for treatment. Not suitable as the main support for people at risk of suicide or self-harm, with psychosis, eating disorders or complex needs.
cautions: General AI chatbots are not designed or regulated as therapy, can give inaccurate or harmful responses, may encourage dependence, and raise privacy concerns. Some lawsuits and inquiries have followed suicides involving chatbots. Only some tools are regulated as medical devices.
uk: Some NHS Talking Therapies services use AI tools for referral and triage; other apps are available privately. Not a regulated profession; check whether a tool is a registered medical device.
checkNotes: Fast-moving area as of late 2026; details of regulation (e.g. US state laws such as Illinois's 2025 ban on AI therapy, Woebot's app closure in 2025) and UK NHS deployments (e.g. Limbic, Wysa) and their medical device status were not fully verified and may change.

name: Neurofeedback
aka: EEG biofeedback; neurotherapy; includes fMRI neurofeedback
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed in digital and technology because it uses brain-recording equipment and computer feedback.
what: A form of biofeedback in which brain activity, usually measured by EEG sensors on the scalp, is shown back to the person in real time through sounds, images or games. The aim is for people to learn to change their brain activity patterns, which is claimed to improve attention, mood or sleep.
origin: Developed from Joe Kamiya's alpha-wave experiments in the US in the early 1960s and Barry Sterman's research at UCLA in the late 1960s on brain rhythms and epilepsy.
evidence: For ADHD, the most studied use, a 2025 meta-analysis of 38 trials found no meaningful benefit when outcomes were rated by people unaware of treatment, suggesting earlier positive results reflected expectations. Evidence for depression, anxiety, PTSD and other conditions is limited and of low quality.
practice: Individual sessions of 30 to 60 minutes, often 20 to 40 sessions, in a clinic or at home with rented equipment. Sensors are placed on the scalp while the person watches a screen or listens to feedback.
suitability: Marketed for ADHD, anxiety, sleep problems, trauma and performance. It is not recommended in NICE guidance on ADHD. Generally low risk, but costly and time-consuming.
cautions: Expensive, with many sessions needed; claims by commercial providers often go beyond the evidence. Practitioners are not regulated in the UK. Some people report headaches or tiredness.
uk: Private clinics only; not usually available on the NHS.
checkNotes: Statement that neurofeedback is not recommended in NICE ADHD guidance (NG87) is based on its absence from the recommendations; not verified against exact wording.

name: MDMA-Assisted
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with psychedelic-assisted approaches because a psychoactive drug is given alongside psychotherapy.
what: A structured course of psychotherapy in which a few sessions are carried out under the influence of MDMA. The drug is thought to reduce fear and increase feelings of trust and openness, which may make it easier to revisit traumatic memories with support from therapists.
origin: Used informally by some US therapists from the late 1970s until MDMA was banned there in 1985; formal trials, mainly for PTSD, were developed from the 2000s by the US charity MAPS and later its spin-off company.
evidence: Two phase 3 trials for PTSD reported larger improvements than therapy with placebo, but concerns about blinding, bias and safety monitoring led the US FDA to decline approval in August 2024 and ask for another trial. The company resubmitted in 2026 without a new trial; no decision had been reported at the time of writing.
practice: In trials: around three preparation sessions, then usually three day-long dosing sessions a month apart with two therapists present, each followed by several integration sessions. Delivered only in research or, abroad, in tightly authorised clinical settings.
suitability: Studied mainly for adults with severe, long-lasting PTSD. People with heart disease, high blood pressure, some psychiatric conditions such as psychosis or bipolar disorder, or on certain medicines are usually excluded. It is not part of NICE guidance.
cautions: MDMA is a Class A, Schedule 1 drug in the UK: possession and supply are illegal outside licensed research. Raised heart rate, blood pressure and temperature can occur; illicit pills are of unknown content. Therapist misconduct has been reported in trials.
uk: Not available on the NHS or legally in private practice. Access in the UK is only through approved clinical research studies.
