checkNotes: 2026 resubmission by the renamed company (Resilient, formerly Lykos) is from news/MAPS reports; FDA acceptance or outcome unknown as of November 2026. Australia has allowed authorised psychiatrists to prescribe MDMA for PTSD since July 2023 (not mentioned in text). Origin year c.1977 is approximate.

name: Psilocybin-Assisted
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with psychedelic-assisted approaches because a psychoactive drug is given alongside psychotherapy.
what: Psychological support combined with one or two doses of psilocybin, the active compound in so-called magic mushrooms. The drug produces several hours of altered perception and emotion; the idea is that, with preparation and follow-up, this can loosen rigid patterns of thinking linked to depression or addiction.
origin: Researched in the 1950s and 1960s before legal restrictions halted most work; modern trials resumed in the 2000s at Johns Hopkins, NYU and Imperial College London, and in company-run studies.
evidence: Trials in treatment-resistant and major depression show rapid, sometimes lasting improvements, and two large phase 3 trials met their main goals; a US marketing application was filed in late 2026. Blinding is difficult, long-term data are limited and some participants have serious adverse reactions. Evidence for addiction and anxiety near the end of life is earlier-stage.
practice: Usually one-to-one: several preparation meetings, then a dosing day of about six to eight hours in a calm room with one or two trained monitors, often with eyes covered and music, followed by integration sessions. Currently delivered within research studies.
suitability: Studied mainly in adults with depression that has not responded to other treatments, and in alcohol use disorder and anxiety in serious illness. People with a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder are usually excluded. Not in NICE guidance.
cautions: Psilocybin is a Schedule 1 controlled drug in the UK; mushrooms are Class A. Risks include intense distress, raised blood pressure, headache and, rarely, lasting perceptual or psychotic symptoms. No psilocybin medicine is licensed in the UK.
uk: Not available on the NHS or in legal private practice. Access is only through approved clinical trials, some run by UK universities and companies.
checkNotes: Compass Pathways completed its FDA application for COMP360 in November 2026 per news reports; approval status unknown. UK government agreed in principle in 2025 to ease research licensing for Schedule 1 drugs; psilocybin itself still Schedule 1. Year 1960 approximate (early psilocybin research c. late 1950s-1960s).

name: Ketamine-Assisted
aka: Ketamine-assisted therapy; distinct from ketamine or esketamine given as a medication alone
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with psychedelic-assisted approaches because a psychoactive drug is given alongside psychotherapy.
what: Psychotherapy combined with doses of ketamine, an anaesthetic that at lower doses causes dissociation and can lift mood quickly. This is different from ketamine or esketamine given purely as an antidepressant medicine: in KAP, the drug experience is used within planned therapy sessions to help people work on problems such as depression or addiction.
origin: Explored as a 'psychedelic' therapy from the 1970s, including in Mexico and later Russia for alcohol dependence; its rapid antidepressant effect was reported in the US in 2000, and KAP clinics spread in the 2010s.
evidence: Ketamine itself has good trial evidence for rapid but often short-lived relief of severe depression. Evidence that adding psychotherapy improves or extends this is much thinner: small trials, including a UK trial in alcohol use disorder, are promising, and larger trials are under way.
practice: Typically a medical assessment, then a course of several dosing sessions (injection, infusion or lozenge) in a clinic, with a therapist present or therapy sessions before and after. Delivered by doctors working with therapists, mostly in private clinics.
suitability: Mainly offered to adults with depression that has not responded to standard treatment, and studied in alcohol use disorder and PTSD. Not usually suitable for people with psychosis, uncontrolled high blood pressure or a history of ketamine misuse. Esketamine nasal spray is licensed but NICE has not recommended it for routine NHS use.
cautions: Ketamine is a Class B, Schedule 2 controlled drug in the UK, used off-label for depression. Risks include dissociation, raised blood pressure, misuse and, with heavy repeated use, bladder damage. Quality and supervision vary between private clinics.
uk: Mostly through private clinics or research trials; the NHS rarely offers it outside specialist services. Check the prescriber is GMC-registered and any therapist is on an accredited register.
checkNotes: Origin attribution (Salvador Roquet, Mexico, 1970s; Krupitsky, Russia) and year 1973 are approximate. NICE esketamine decision (final appraisal 2022, not recommended) - not verified whether revisited since. ACMD advised in January 2026 against moving ketamine to Class A; government decision not confirmed.

name: Psychedelic Integration
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with psychedelic-assisted approaches because it focuses on making sense of psychedelic experiences, though no drug is given.
what: Talking support for people who have had, or plan to have, a psychedelic experience, for example in a ceremony abroad, a trial or recreationally. No drugs are provided. The aim is to help people understand and process what happened, reduce risks and cope with any lasting distress, using a harm-reduction rather than an encouraging stance.
origin: The idea of 'integration' comes from 1960s psychedelic research; as a distinct service it developed from the 2010s alongside harm-reduction groups, psychedelic research and the spread of retreats.
evidence: There are almost no trials of integration as a stand-alone therapy. Integration sessions are a standard part of psychedelic research protocols, but their separate contribution has not been tested. Its value rests mainly on general counselling and harm-reduction principles.
practice: Usually one-to-one or in peer groups, often weekly for a few sessions, sometimes online. Delivered by counsellors, psychotherapists or peer facilitators who draw on existing approaches such as person-centred, mindfulness-based or trauma-informed work.
suitability: People troubled or confused by a past psychedelic experience, or wanting to reduce risks. It is not a treatment for psychosis or a substitute for medical help in a crisis. Not covered by NICE guidance.
cautions: In the UK, therapists must not supply drugs or arrange illegal use; legitimate practice stays within harm reduction. The field is unregulated, so training varies. Persistent perceptual changes, panic or psychotic symptoms need medical assessment.
uk: Private practitioners and some charities or peer groups. Check membership of an accredited register (such as BACP or UKCP); integration itself has no recognised qualification.
checkNotes: No single founder or founding date; year left null. Evidence statement reflects absence of known trials rather than a systematic review.

name: Reiki
what: A Japanese-derived practice in which a practitioner places hands lightly on or just above a clothed person's body. Practitioners describe channelling a universal life energy to promote relaxation and healing; this energy has not been shown to exist.
origin: Developed by Mikao Usui in Japan in the early 1920s; brought to the West via Hawaii by Hawayo Takata from the late 1930s.
evidence: Reviews, including a Cochrane review on anxiety and depression, find too few good-quality trials to show a specific benefit. Some people report feeling calmer, which is consistent with relaxation, attention and expectation rather than an energy effect.
practice: Usually one-to-one sessions of about an hour, lying clothed on a couch, sometimes offered as 'distance Reiki'. Delivered by practitioners trained in levels or 'attunements'; some hospices and hospitals offer it as complementary care.
suitability: Some people use it for relaxation or comfort, including during serious illness. It is not a treatment for mental health conditions and is not recommended in NICE guidance.
cautions: Generally physically safe, but should not replace effective treatment. Light touch may be unwelcome for some trauma survivors; consent should be clear. Not statutorily regulated.
uk: Private practitioners and some hospices. A voluntary register exists through the Complementary and Natural Healthcare Council (CNHC); this does not imply proof of effectiveness.

name: Pranic Healing
what: A no-touch energy practice in which the practitioner moves their hands near the body to 'scan', 'cleanse' and 'energise' an energy field said to be made of prana, or life force. Its proposed mechanism is not supported by science.
origin: Developed by Choa Kok Sui, a Filipino businessman and teacher, who popularised it through books and courses from 1987.
evidence: There is no credible trial evidence that pranic healing has specific effects on mental or physical health. Published studies are few, small and mostly by supporters, with high risk of bias.
practice: Usually one-to-one sessions of around 30 to 60 minutes, sitting or standing, clothed, with no contact; also group meditations such as 'twin hearts'. Delivered by practitioners trained through the founder's organisations.
suitability: Used by some for relaxation or as part of spiritual practice. It is not a treatment for any mental health condition and does not appear in NICE guidance.
cautions: Not regulated in the UK. Main risk is delaying effective treatment. Be wary of costly course structures or claims to treat serious illness.
uk: Private practitioners and centres linked to the founder's organisations. No NHS provision and no statutory regulation.

name: Chakra Balancing
what: A practice based on the idea that the body has a series of energy centres, or chakras, along the spine that can become 'blocked' or 'unbalanced'. Practitioners use touch, meditation, sound, colour or crystals to restore balance. Chakras have no anatomical or physiological basis.
origin: The chakra concept comes from ancient Indian tantric and yogic traditions; the modern seven-chakra 'balancing' practice is largely a 20th-century Western adaptation popular in New Age circles.
evidence: There is no credible evidence that chakras exist as described or that balancing them affects mental health. Any benefit people report is likely to come from relaxation, meditation or the attention of the practitioner.
practice: One-to-one sessions, often an hour, combining guided meditation, breathing, hands-on or hands-off work, sound bowls or stones. Also offered as group classes or in yoga settings. Delivered by self-employed practitioners with varied training.
suitability: Some people value it as a spiritual or relaxation practice. It is not a treatment for mental health conditions and is not in NICE guidance.
cautions: Not regulated. Should not delay effective care. In its original Indian traditions the chakras are religious concepts, and commercial versions often simplify them.
uk: Private practitioners, holistic centres and yoga studios. No NHS provision.
checkNotes: Ancient origin, so year left null; date of the modern Western form is approximate.

name: Crystal Healing
what: A practice in which crystals or gemstones are placed on or around the body, held or worn, on the belief that each stone carries properties that can affect energy, mood or health. There is no known mechanism by which this could work.
origin: Ideas about the powers of stones are ancient and found in many cultures; the modern practice grew out of the New Age movement in the US and UK in the 1970s and 1980s.
evidence: There is no credible evidence of specific benefit. A small experiment found people reported similar sensations whether holding real or fake crystals, pointing to suggestion and expectation.
practice: One-to-one sessions of about an hour, lying down while stones are arranged on the body, often with relaxation or meditation. Also self-practice with purchased crystals. Delivered by practitioners with varied, unregulated training.
suitability: Some people use it for relaxation or meaning. It is not a treatment for any mental health condition and is not in NICE guidance.
cautions: Unregulated. Main risk is relying on it instead of effective help, and cost. Some crystals are mined in ways that raise ethical and environmental concerns.
uk: Private practitioners and holistic shops or centres. No NHS provision.
checkNotes: Ancient roots; year null. The placebo-crystal experiment (Christopher French and colleagues, 2001) was a conference presentation, so not named.

name: Shamanic Healing
what: Healing practices inspired by shamanic traditions, in which a practitioner enters an altered state, often through drumming, to 'journey' and seek help from spirits, for example by 'soul retrieval'. Western versions usually borrow from many cultures, and their spiritual claims cannot be tested scientifically.
origin: Shamanic practices are ancient and found worldwide. The widespread Western form, 'core shamanism', was popularised by US anthropologist Michael Harner, notably through his 1980 book.
evidence: There is little trial evidence for clinical mental-health outcomes; small studies are low quality. People may find meaning, community and relaxation in it, but it has not been shown to treat mental health conditions.
practice: One-to-one sessions or group workshops, often lasting one to two hours, with drumming, rattles, guided 'journeys' and ritual. Delivered by self-trained or workshop-trained Western practitioners; traditional shamans work within their own communities.
suitability: Some people value it as a spiritual practice. It is not recommended in NICE guidance, and may not suit people prone to dissociation or psychosis.
cautions: Unregulated. Altered states can be distressing. Some retreats combine it with psychoactive substances such as ayahuasca, which is illegal in the UK and has caused harm. Borrowing from Indigenous cultures raises appropriation concerns.
uk: Private practitioners and workshops. No NHS provision and no statutory regulation.
checkNotes: Evidence level 'limited' rather than 'none' because a few small studies exist; could reasonably be 'none'.

name: Curanderismo
aka: Mexican and Mexican-American traditional healing; healer is a curandero or curandera
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with cultural and indigenous practices because it is a living community healing tradition.
what: A diverse traditional healing system practised in Mexico, parts of Latin America and Mexican-American communities. Healers treat physical, emotional and spiritual problems, including folk illnesses such as susto (fright), using prayer, ritual cleansings (limpias), herbs, massage and counsel. It is a family of practices rooted in particular communities, not a single technique.
origin: Developed over centuries from Indigenous Mesoamerican, Spanish Catholic and African traditions, mainly from the 16th century onwards.
evidence: There is little trial evidence for clinical mental-health outcomes, and judging its spiritual meaning by trial standards has limits. Anthropological research suggests it can offer culturally meaningful support and community, and some health services work alongside curanderos.
practice: Usually one-to-one or with family present, in the healer's home or a community setting. Sessions vary widely and may include prayer, egg or herb cleansings, herbal remedies and advice. Healers are often recognised by their community rather than formally trained.
suitability: Most meaningful to people from the communities where it is rooted. It is not in NICE guidance and is not a replacement for treatment of serious mental illness.
cautions: Some herbal remedies can interact with medicines or be toxic. Practised outside its communities, it risks appropriation and commercialisation. Not regulated in the UK.
uk: Very limited in the UK; mainly within Latin American communities or through private practitioners. No NHS provision.
checkNotes: Traditional practice, year null. Scope of UK availability not verified.

name: Native American Healing
aka: Indigenous North American healing; traditional Native healing
familyNote: The source does not state its family; it is placed with cultural and indigenous practices because it refers to the healing traditions of Indigenous peoples of North America.
what: An umbrella term for the many distinct healing traditions of hundreds of Indigenous nations in North America. These often treat wellbeing as a balance of body, mind, spirit, community and land, and may involve ceremony, prayer, plant medicines, talking circles and the sweat lodge. They belong to specific communities and are not a single technique.
origin: Ancient and continuing traditions, held by particular nations and passed on through elders and healers. Many were suppressed in the US and Canada until legal protections from the late 1970s.
evidence: There is little trial evidence for clinical mental-health outcomes, and trial methods fit these practices poorly. Studies in Indigenous communities suggest that culturally based programmes can support recovery from addiction and trauma, often alongside conventional care.
practice: Varies by nation: one-to-one work with a recognised healer or medicine person, family involvement, community ceremonies and circles. Some Indigenous-led health services in North America combine traditional healing with clinical treatment.
suitability: Most meaningful to Indigenous people within their own communities. Not in NICE guidance and not designed as a treatment for people outside those traditions.
cautions: Many commercial 'Native American' ceremonies outside Indigenous communities are imitations; people have died in poorly run sweat lodges, including three in Arizona in 2009. Taking ceremonies out of context is widely regarded as appropriation.
uk: Authentic practice is essentially unavailable in the UK. Workshops using the label are private, unregulated and usually not connected to Indigenous communities.
checkNotes: The 2009 Arizona sweat lodge deaths were at a self-help retreat run by a non-Native leader. Legal protection reference is to the US American Indian Religious Freedom Act 1978; Canadian changes differ in timing.

name: Primal Scream
what: A therapy built on the idea that neurosis comes from repressed pain from early life, including birth. Clients were encouraged to re-experience and discharge this 'primal pain', often by crying or screaming, in the belief that this would release it for good.
origin: Developed by US psychologist Arthur Janov in Los Angeles in the late 1960s, and made famous by his 1970 book The Primal Scream and by celebrity clients.
evidence: There are no good-quality trials showing benefit. Research on emotional 'venting' suggests that expressing anger in this way can increase rather than reduce it. The theory of stored birth trauma is not supported.
practice: Originally an intensive start of daily sessions over about three weeks, often open-ended in length, followed by group sessions, in a padded or soundproofed room. A small number of practitioners still offer versions of it privately.
suitability: Not recommended in any NICE guidance. Intense regression may be harmful for people with trauma histories, psychosis or fragile mental health.
cautions: Can be emotionally overwhelming and intensive formats are costly. Practitioners are not regulated as such; mainstream professional bodies do not endorse it.
uk: Not available on the NHS. Very few private practitioners; not a recognised training route on UK accredited registers.
checkNotes: Status 'retired' reflects mainstream disuse, although a few practitioners continue.

name: Orgone Therapy
what: Wilhelm Reich's later theory that a universal life energy, which he called orgone, flows through the body and that blocked orgone causes psychological and physical illness. Treatment included body-focused work on 'muscular armour' and sitting in an 'orgone accumulator', a box of layered materials. Orgone has never been shown to exist.
origin: Developed by Austrian psychoanalyst Wilhelm Reich in the late 1930s and 1940s, first in Norway and then in the US, building on his earlier character analysis.
evidence: There is no credible evidence that orgone exists or that accumulators work. A US court banned their interstate sale in 1954 after the FDA found the claims false. Reich's earlier ideas about the body influenced later body psychotherapies, which are judged separately.
practice: Historically individual sessions involving breathing, touch and work on muscle tension, plus use of accumulators. A small group of orgonomists in the US continues the tradition.
suitability: Not recommended for any condition and not in NICE guidance.
cautions: Claims to treat serious illness such as cancer are unfounded. Reich was jailed in 1956 for contempt of the court order and died in prison in 1957.
uk: Not available on the NHS. Not a recognised practice on UK accredited registers; related body psychotherapies are offered privately.

name: Rebirthing
aka: Rebirthing breathwork (Leonard Orr); separately, 'rebirthing' as a coercive attachment therapy
what: The name covers two different things. Rebirthing breathwork uses connected, rapid breathing to 'relive' birth and release supposed birth trauma. Separately, some unregulated 'attachment therapists' used 'rebirthing' to physically re-enact birth with children, wrapping them tightly, in the belief that this would create a bond with adoptive parents.
origin: Rebirthing breathwork was developed by Leonard Orr in California in the mid-1970s. 'Rebirthing' attachment techniques emerged within a fringe US attachment-therapy movement in the 1990s.
evidence: There is no credible evidence for either form. The attachment version caused a death: in 2000, ten-year-old Candace Newmaker suffocated in Colorado while wrapped in blankets during a 'rebirthing' session; two therapists were convicted. Rapid breathing can cause dizziness and tingling and may trigger panic.
practice: Breathwork: individual or group sessions of one to two hours, lying down and breathing in a continuous rhythm with a facilitator, sometimes in water. The coercive attachment version is condemned and should not be practised.
suitability: Not recommended for any condition and not in NICE guidance. Breathwork may not suit people with heart or lung problems, epilepsy, pregnancy, panic disorder or psychosis.
cautions: Any therapy that restrains, wraps or coerces a child is dangerous and is rejected by professional bodies. Breathwork is unregulated. Colorado banned rebirthing after Candace Newmaker's death.
uk: Not available on the NHS. Breathwork workshops exist privately and are unregulated.
checkNotes: Year 1974 is the approximate start of Orr's rebirthing breathwork.

name: EST
aka: Assumed here to mean est, the large-group awareness training; not ECT (electroconvulsive therapy)
what: A large-group 'awareness training' that ran over two weekends, using long sessions, confrontation and strict rules to get participants to 'take responsibility' for their lives and drop beliefs said to hold them back. It was not a psychotherapy as such, though it was marketed for personal growth.
origin: Founded by Werner Erhard in San Francisco in 1971. It was replaced in 1985 by 'The Forum', which later became the Landmark Forum, run by a different company.
evidence: There is no good trial evidence of mental-health benefit. Some participants reported feeling better; others, including people with existing mental illness, have been reported to suffer psychiatric crises after intense large-group trainings.
practice: Groups of a few hundred people in a hotel ballroom for about 60 hours over two weekends, led by a trainer, with restricted breaks and personal sharing. Successor programmes run similar weekend courses.
suitability: Not a treatment for any mental health condition and not in NICE guidance. Intense confrontational formats may be harmful for people who are vulnerable.
cautions: If 'EST' was meant to refer to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), that is not retired: ECT is a current treatment that NICE recognises for severe depression and some other severe conditions, given under anaesthesia with consent safeguards.
uk: est itself no longer runs. Successor large-group courses operate privately and are unregulated. ECT is available through NHS psychiatric services.
checkNotes: Ambiguous name. In a list beside primal scream, orgone and rebirthing, 'EST' most plausibly means Erhard Seminars Training; it could alternatively mean electroshock therapy (ECT), which is current, not retired. NICE ECT guidance (TA59 and NG222) stated from knowledge, not re-verified online.

name: Psychosurgery
aka: Lobotomy; prefrontal leucotomy; modern form called neurosurgery for mental disorder
what: Brain surgery intended to treat mental illness by cutting or destroying connections in the brain, most notoriously the prefrontal lobotomy. It was meant to reduce severe agitation, distress or obsessions, but often did so by blunting personality and functioning.
origin: Introduced by Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz in Lisbon in 1935, who later received a Nobel Prize; spread widely in the US by Walter Freeman and James Watts, including the 'ice-pick' transorbital method from 1946.
evidence: Lobotomy caused deaths, epilepsy, lasting cognitive and personality damage and was often done without meaningful consent. It declined from the mid-1950s as antipsychotic drugs arrived. Very rare, precisely targeted modern procedures for severe, treatment-resistant depression or OCD have limited evidence.
practice: Historically performed on tens of thousands of people in asylums, often quickly and with little follow-up. Today, in the UK, only a handful of highly selected patients each year are considered, in specialist neurosurgical centres after exhaustive assessment.
suitability: Lobotomy is not used. Modern neurosurgery for mental disorder is considered only for severe, chronic depression or OCD that has not responded to every other treatment.
cautions: In England and Wales, surgery that destroys brain tissue for mental disorder requires the patient's valid consent and independent approval under section 57 of the Mental Health Act 1983; Scotland has similar safeguards.
uk: Lobotomy is not performed. Very rare modern procedures are available only through specialist NHS centres with Mental Health Act safeguards.
checkNotes: Section 57 MHA 1983 stated from knowledge (requires consent plus certification by a second-opinion doctor and two others); not re-verified online. Deep brain stimulation is not destructive and is regulated differently.

name: Insulin Shock
aka: Insulin coma therapy; deep insulin therapy
what: A treatment, mainly for schizophrenia, in which patients were injected with large doses of insulin to put them into a hypoglycaemic coma, repeated daily over weeks. It was thought that the comas somehow reset the brain.
origin: Introduced by Austrian psychiatrist Manfred Sakel, who began in Berlin in the late 1920s and published his method in Vienna in 1933; widely used in Europe and the US until the late 1950s.
evidence: Its apparent benefits were not confirmed: a 1950s controlled comparison found similar results with barbiturate-induced unconsciousness, and critics noted that the extra attention patients received could explain improvement. It carried a significant risk of death and brain damage.
practice: Courses of around 50 to 60 comas, five or six days a week, on specialist 'insulin units', with nurses monitoring patients and ending each coma with glucose. Abandoned in favour of antipsychotic drugs.
suitability: Not used for any condition today.
cautions: Caused deaths, prolonged coma, brain damage and obesity. Historical interest only.
uk: Not available. It was abandoned in UK hospitals by the 1960s.
checkNotes: The 1950s controlled comparison is the Ackner and Oldham trial (1957); not named in text.

name: Hydrotherapy
aka: Asylum hydrotherapy: continuous baths, wet sheet packs; not modern physiotherapy hydrotherapy
what: The use of water in asylums and psychiatric hospitals to calm agitated or distressed patients, mainly through prolonged warm baths lasting hours or days and tightly wrapped wet sheet packs. It was believed to soothe the nervous system. This is different from modern hydrotherapy, which is exercise in a warm pool used in physiotherapy.
origin: Water cures were popularised in the 1820s and 1830s by Vincenz Priessnitz in Silesia; psychiatric hydrotherapy was common in asylums from the late 19th century until the 1940s and 1950s.
evidence: It was never tested in controlled trials. Patients could be calmer, but packs and baths were often used as restraint, and burns, chilling and distress were reported. Modern pool-based physiotherapy has its own evidence for physical conditions.
practice: Patients were placed in baths with canvas covers for hours or wrapped in cold, wet sheets until warmed, supervised by attendants. It declined with the arrival of sedative and antipsychotic medicines.
suitability: Not used as a psychiatric treatment today. Modern hydrotherapy pools are used for musculoskeletal and neurological rehabilitation.
cautions: Historical use as restraint without consent. Unrelated to modern aquatic physiotherapy, which is delivered by HCPC-registered physiotherapists.
uk: Historical psychiatric hydrotherapy is not available. Modern pool-based hydrotherapy is offered by NHS and private physiotherapy services.
checkNotes: Year 1890 is a rough marker for widespread asylum use. 'Harmful' evidence level reflects documented injury and use as restraint rather than large-scale deaths; 'limited' would also be defensible.

name: Mesmerism
what: An 18th-century treatment based on the idea of an invisible natural force, 'animal magnetism', flowing through living things. Practitioners used passes of the hands, gazing and magnetised objects to provoke a 'crisis' that was thought to restore the flow and cure illness.
origin: Developed by German physician Franz Anton Mesmer in Vienna in the 1770s and made fashionable in Paris from 1778.
evidence: A French royal commission in 1784, including Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier, tested it and concluded that the effects came from imagination, not a magnetic fluid. It is regarded as an early demonstration of suggestion and placebo.
practice: Historically, groups sat around a tub of 'magnetised' water holding iron rods, or received individual passes from the mesmerist, sometimes falling into convulsions or trance.
suitability: Not used today. Its study of trance led, through James Braid in the 1840s, to hypnosis, which is assessed separately.
uk: Not available as a treatment. Modern clinical hypnosis is offered privately and occasionally within the NHS.
checkNotes: Year 1775 approximate (Mesmer's first writings on animal magnetism c.1774-1779).

name: Phrenology-Based
what: A 19th-century theory that the mind is made up of separate faculties located in specific brain 'organs', and that their size can be read from bumps on the skull. Phrenologists offered character readings and advice on self-improvement, education and choosing a spouse or job.
origin: Developed by German physician Franz Joseph Gall in Vienna around 1796, spread by Johann Spurzheim and, in Britain, by George Combe in Edinburgh from the 1820s.
evidence: Phrenology has been disproved: skull shape does not reflect brain structure or character. It was also used to support racist and sexist claims. Its one lasting contribution was the general idea that different brain regions have different functions.
practice: Historically a phrenologist felt the head and measured the skull, then gave a written chart of strengths and weaknesses with advice. It was popular as public entertainment and self-help.
suitability: Not used today for any purpose.
cautions: Its use to justify racial and social hierarchies caused real harm.
uk: Not available. Historical collections can be seen in some UK museums.
